Al-Razi said: it was named thus either because of its being visible to the eye, or because of the intensity of its flow, from the (phrase) "im'an fi al-sayr" (going far in travel), or because of its abundance, from "al-ma'n," which is the abundant; and al-ma'un (utensils) was named so for the great benefit derived from it; and it is said: "mashrab mamun" (a drink that is abundant), meaning one that hardly ever ceases.

When it came to drink, the first thing one chooses is its colour, then its taste. So He said, describing what is in the cup of wine as something to be served: ﴿white﴾; that is, shining and pure, extremely delicate, sparkling with light. He went to great lengths in describing it as good by making it an explanation of the meaning in His saying: ﴿delicious to those who drink﴾, with what they used to swallow of the cups of sorrows and distresses. He made the place of the pronoun explicit, for generality and for tying the judgment to the description (p-231). He also used the plural to indicate that they will drink it only in this way, with its added delight.

When he had attributed perfection to it, he negated imperfection from it, saying: ﴿There is no ghoul in it﴾, meaning: no corruption, such as a headache, loosening of the joints, or a burning of the liver, or anything else that *yaghtal* (destroys), that is, that causes ruin or becomes a cause of ruin. ﴿Nor will they be drained by it﴾, meaning: as a habit after drinking it, ﴿yunzafun﴾ (are drained), meaning some of their minds depart, even if they drink long and much; so that their delight does not diminish and their drink does not run out, or the wealth they possess for everything that gives them pleasure does not run out.

According to the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i, with a *kasra* on the *zay*, from *anzafa* (in the active voice), like *aqalla* and *a'sara*, when a man becomes poor in wealth or his mind departs. The reading of the majority (*qira'ah*, a canonical recitation) with the passive form may be from *nazafa*. In that case it may mean the drink runs out, from the saying "*nazafat al-rakiyyah*" (the well ran dry), meaning its water departed. It may also mean the departure of the mind, from the saying "*nazafa al-rajul*" (active) and "*nuzifa*" (passive), meaning his mind departed because of intoxication. It may also be from *anzafa*, and in that case it may mean the departure of the mind, from "*anzafa al-rajul*" when his mind departed through intoxication; or it may mean the absence of drink, from the saying "*nazafa al-rajul al-khamrah*" (the man drained the wine), whether the verb is active or passive, when he has exhausted it. [p. 232]

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 48:

Since all of that cannot be complete except through intercourse (al-jima'), and wine is the thing most conducive to it, and since bliss is not complete with it except through exclusivity (al-ikhtisas), He said: ﴿And with them﴾ are women from the people of this world and others, ﴿restraining their glances﴾, i.e., not one of them glances toward anyone other than her husband, and the extremity of her beauty and the abundance of her loveliness do not leave him glancing toward anyone else, ﴿with wide, lovely eyes﴾, i.e., with large, beautiful eyes, the plural of "ʿaynaʾ" (large-eyed); its ʿayn was broken to match the yā' (ʿīn).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 49:

Since the finest of colours, especially in the eyes of the Arabs, is white tinged with red, and a yellowness that gives it clarity, radiance and beauty, He said: ﴿As if they were eggs﴾; that is, ostrich eggs; ﴿well-guarded﴾; that is, protected from any soiling that might touch them and any dust that might cover them. Because of the Arabs' love for this colour, they would describe women as "white-skinned ones of the curtained chambers" (bayḍāt al-khudūr), since its colour is white tinged with a pure yellowness. Imru' al-Qays expressed this explicitly in his famous Lamiyya, where he said:

"Like a maiden whose whiteness is mingled with yellow, nourished by water from a pure spring, unmixed."

(p-233) That is: mingled with whiteness inclining towards redness, with yellow. It is the purest and most balanced of colours, resembling the colour of the light of the moon.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 50:

When that gathering was for the sake of joy, and joy is not complete except through companionship, and the sweetest companionship is that which reminds one of the arrival of a blessing or the removal of a calamity, there necessarily follows from this His saying, indicating the tranquility of mind and soundness of reason, and correctness in speech: ﴿So some of them turned to others, questioning one another.﴾ That is, the people of Paradise, with speech. He also indicated that the mere turning toward someone with intent draws hearts to listen to him, by the particle of elevation (ʿalā, "upon"), so He said: ﴿upon one another﴾. That is, for the sake of the speech which is the spirit of that station. As for facing one another, it has already been mentioned that it is constant. He then explained the state of this turning, so He said: ﴿questioning one another﴾. That is, they converse in a clear discourse, in which nothing is obscure, with what the manifest expression indicates, namely that it is a matter which ought to be cared for and inquired about, concerning their circumstances from which they were delivered after they had nearly been brought to ruin. He called it "questioning" because, although it is fitting that they be asked about it, it is not free of a question whose least form is that the listener to the conversation attends to the talk. He expressed it in the past tense to indicate its certainty, as the certainty of what has already occurred.

When the listener became eager to hear something from them that would serve as a model for the rest, he pointed to this by his saying, as a fresh (*isti'naf*, resumptive) statement: ﴿A speaker among them says﴾; i.e., in this questioning. And how far apart this is from the account of the questioning of the people of the Fire that came earlier!

Since he had thought that he would not be freed from the evil of that companion who is being spoken of, and God saved him from it, contrary to what appeared, which was one of the great blessings, he drew attention to it with emphasis, saying: ﴿Indeed, I had a companion﴾; i.e., a companion from among the people, as if he were a manifest devil.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 52:

﴿Yaqūlu﴾ (he says): i.e., denying the resurrection, deeming it extremely unlikely, renewing his statement at every moment. He wants to deceive me, by the gentleness of his guidance, toward his evil belief. ﴿Āinnaka la-mina al-muṣaddiqīna﴾ (Are you indeed among those who affirm it?): i.e., of the resurrection. He reproaches me with this, and belittles my insight in considering it, so as to stir up my resolve and inflame my pride and my zeal.

He repeats the denial with his saying: ﴿Is it that when we have died﴾; that is, our souls have departed; ﴿and have become﴾; that is, a settled state; ﴿dust and bones﴾; that is, our bodies, which are the vehicles of the souls, have been crushed to nothing; ﴿Are we indeed to be recompensed?﴾; that is, are we indeed to be requited after that for what we did; by being resurrected and repaid. His emphasis (with inna and lam) was an indication, from him, to every intelligent person who is inclined to deny what I have affirmed, because of its remoteness; or an indication that he himself denies it, even though it is emphasized.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 54:

When this statement was a cause for the listener's great eagerness to know what would follow it; and since the people of Paradise, by the height of their station, their rank, the soundness of their bodies, the strength of their constitution, and the penetrating power of their sight, such that they look at whatever they wish of the Fire and other things beneath them, whenever they wish; he resumed his speech, indicating that this state of his makes it known that he is among the people of the Fire: ﴿He said﴾; i.e., this speaker, addressing those who drink with him, who are, as one of them said in a muwashshah:

Many a company arranged like a necklace,
clothed in garments whose embroidery is generosity.

I seized the pleasure as they seized it,
and the cups among them I considered...

Stars in the sky of delight are seen,
each star sets in the full moon.

﴿Would you look down?﴾; i.e., would you be kind enough to set my heart at ease by leaving what you are in of the perfection of pleasure, and by taking the trouble to look with me into the Fire, so that you might gladden me by that.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 55:

Since the one spoken of (al-muhaddath 'anhu) is the sincere ones (al-mukhlisin), who are all of the people of Paradise, or most of them, and since the pronoun refers back to what precedes it exactly, and since the addressees of this speaker are only his drinking companions, and since it is known from what has passed of mutual facing, affection, and association through companionship and mutual questioning, that they eagerly turn to him and surely attend to him, and since the beneficial part for us is only his speech alone, in rebuking his enemy and making his own soul and his friend envy (taghbit), he did not make the pronoun plural, lest it cause confusion (yulbis) and give the impression that it is for everyone; and he returned it to him alone, so that we may take heed from his words and be admonished by what he related to us of his state. So he said: ﴿Then he looked down﴾; meaning: by reason of what he saw for himself of great pleasure in that, toward the people of the Fire; ﴿and saw him﴾; meaning: that bad companion; ﴿in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾; meaning: in its middle and its depths, blazing around him with the most intense blazing, in return for what he used to kindle in his heart in the world of heat, every time he spoke that statement to him. And he called the middle "sawa'" because of the equal distance from it to the sides, like the center of a circle.

Then he resumed the report of his recompense for what had passed of his reproach and rebuke for believing in the Hereafter, by saying: ﴿He said﴾; that is, to his companion, that. And since it would not occur to anyone's mind that he had paid any heed to this statement of his, because it was obviously false, and because this speaker is judged to be among the people of Paradise, He emphasized his statement, indicating that his words often had an effect upon him, through what Satan adorns for him and what souls find pleasing through desires and ease from the burden of acts of obedience. He introduced it in the style of an oath, to draw attention to the wonder at his safety from it, so He said: ﴿By God﴾. He added to the emphasis, after attaching it to the Greatest Name, by using the lightened form of the heavy particle, so He said: ﴿Indeed, you were close to ruining me﴾; that is, you came close to destroying me and placing me in the most wretched of places. In this emphasis is the utmost encouragement to steadfastness for one who is near to being shaken, and to keeping far from evil companions.

Since he had mentioned the evil that used to come from his companion, he mentioned the good effect of God (glorified is He) upon him. So he said, turning the speech to the attribute of benevolence, because it is its station:

﴿Had it not been for the grace of my Lord﴾; that is, the One who was good to me, by what He nurtured me with of making me firm against following you, and overlooking my association with you; ﴿I would surely have been﴾; a settled state; ﴿among those brought forward﴾ (p-237), that is, those compelled to attend this distressing place in which you are. Glory be to God! How great is the benefit of this verse in warning against keeping company with evil companions, for it is extremely dangerous and its effect is ugly! His this observation shows that he had no greater pleasure than what he was in; so he was not lower than it, for there is nothing more pleasant than seeing a cunning enemy who has long burned hearts and confused minds, in such denial and great troubles, from the flames of Hell.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 58:

When he saw that (the other) in the state he was in of the blazing fire (al-jahim), and saw himself in the state he was in of bliss (al-na'im), he could not restrain himself from saying, as happens to one who is in hardship and then relief comes to him suddenly, so that he becomes as though in a dream, or a confusion of dreams, not believing what has come to him, out of joy: ﴿Are we then not﴾; that is: "Are we, my brothers, indulged and made to abide (forever)?" Then, as a consequence of that, (he said) that "we are not ﴿dying﴾"; that is, after this state of ours. And he emphasized it, because the like of this, on account of its preciousness, is hardly believed.

Then he went to the extreme in generality with that which is its criterion; so he said: ﴿Except our first death﴾; that is: the one which occurred in the world.

When he mentioned the blessing of deliverance from death, he mentioned the blessing of rescue from troubles; so he said: ﴿And we will not be﴾; and he emphasized the negation, so he said: ﴿punished﴾.

When he remembered this, joy stirred him and delight and happiness overcame him, he could not contain himself from saying—using the style of emphasis because of the liveliness this had for him and because of the breaking of custom it involved, drawing attention to its greatness and to magnify his delight—: ﴿Indeed, this﴾; that is, the kingdom in which we are; ﴿is surely the great triumph﴾; that is, by itself alone; ﴿the great triumph﴾; that is, the one nothing equals.

Since this context has shown the greatness of what they attained, he increased its magnification by saying: ﴿For the like of this let the workers work﴾; that is, of the reward; ﴿let the workers work﴾; that is, so that they may attain it; for they will be enriched with a richness after which there is no poverty, unlike what they compete for and vie with one another over in the affairs of this world; for it, along with its swift passing away, is spoiled by its turbidity and its tedium.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 62:

When the description had gone beyond this arousing of desire for this bliss, he (Allah) cast at its description another throw, one that outran the intellects, exceeded the limit of comprehension, and rose above the imagining of the fancy. It took the form of a rhetorical question that repels from its opposite, in proportion to the encouragement toward the bliss for whoever has understanding (lubb). So He said: ﴿Is that﴾, the reward, far to attain and unique in its likeness, ﴿better as a welcome gift (nuzul)?﴾ By this He indicated that it is merely something small, as a welcome is offered to a guest upon his arrival, in comparison with what appears beside what lies for them beyond that, which the intellects cannot contain and the understandings cannot grasp. ﴿Or the tree of zaqqum?﴾, that is, the one you know to be in the extreme of foulness and bitterness, from their saying "tazaqqama al-ta'am" (he swallowed the food), when he takes it with dislike and great difficulty. He equated between things that have no equivalence at all, as a warning about this. And because they used to see that the deeds which caused that (the zaqqum) were better than the deeds of the believers, which had caused them bliss, it was as if they were saying: "This punishment is better than the bliss." So that was recited in this manner as a rebuke to them for their poor choice.

[p. 239]

Since He had informed them that its growth was in the Fire, that became a cause for increasing their denial, because their not believing was a cause of narrowness in their minds. He said, emphasizing, as a rebuttal to those who think that He, glory be to Him, does not test His servants because He is free of need for that:

﴿Indeed, We made it﴾; that is, the tree; by virtue of Our majesty; ﴿a trial for the wrongdoers﴾; that is, those who place things in other than their proper places; ﴿like one who is in darkness﴾; by its being a punishment for them in the Hereafter and a cause of increasing their misguidance in this world. Had they placed it in its proper place, they would have known that He who made within the green tree a fire that does not burn it, and who brings them out whenever they wish so that they burn with it whatever wood or other things they want, is able to make a green tree grow in the Fire that the Fire does not burn.

Then he drew attention to the fact that the locus of the trial lies in making it something they deny. So he said (Exalted is He), emphasizing it because of their denial, giving the reason for making it a trial, one that mingles with them so that in this world it destroys them by its heat, and in the next by its effect: ﴿Indeed, it﴾; and he confirmed the matter of its growth by saying: ﴿a tree﴾; and he increased the matter's clarity by saying: ﴿that springs forth﴾; and he reinforced it with the adverbial phrase, saying: ﴿from the root﴾; that is, the firmly established base, the depths, the core, and the settled place of ﴿Hellfire (al-Jahim)﴾; that is, the fire of intense blazing, whose branches rise up to its levels.

Then he increased this clarity and depiction by His saying: ﴿Its shoots﴾ (ṭalʿuhā), that is, what is like the shoots of the date palm in its growth, then its splitting open to reveal its fruit; ﴿as if they were the heads of the devils﴾ (ruʾūs al-shayāṭīn), concerning which the addressees have an image of it, namely the ugliness that has reached its extreme. This simile falls in its most complete place, whether the shayṭān (devil) for them was a name for a serpent or for something else, because the ugliness of the devils and what is connected to them, in that they are pure evil unmixed with any good, is established in souls. For this reason, everyone who found a person's appearance or action repulsive would say: "He looks like a devil," just as the goodness and majesty of the angels have become impressed upon souls, so beautiful forms were imagined for them. Likewise, the Arabs named the fruit of a tree called al-Astan (a bitter, thorny plant) by this name, and it is a rough, bitter, foul-smelling tree of hideous appearance.

Since he had established the matter of this tree with what is most intensely a trial for them, and a gentle test for the believers, he caused the trial through it to follow with His words, refuting their denial that they should eat of what they do not desire, and contradicting what they used to claim of repelling it: ﴿Indeed, they﴾; that is, because of their disbelief in it and in other things that God had commanded them, ﴿will surely eat from it﴾; that is, from this tree, from its thorns and its spathes (ṭalʿ), and whatever God wills of what causes pain from it. And since they had exaggerated in mocking its matter, He increased the emphasis in response to that with His words: ﴿and fill (their) bellies with it﴾; and with other than it, at that time when God wills their eating of it, ﴿the bellies﴾ (p-241) by compulsion upon that and forcibly; and when He burned their livers from severe hunger, as an increase in the punishment.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 67:

When it is the habit that the affluent eater, after his meal, takes a dessert of something that cools the burning of his liver, He said, indicating the extreme foulness of their dessert and the long blazing of their thirst, with the particle of delay (thumma) and the instrument of emphasis (inna), because of the great denial contained in that: ﴿Then indeed for them upon it﴾; that is, upon their eating from it; ﴿surely a mixture﴾; that is, a mixture of greatly burning quality; ﴿of boiling water﴾; that is, hot water; as if it were a compound of waters from various extracts, of pus, and filth, and the like. We ask Allah for well-being.

When what was mentioned for the two groups was only the *nuzul* (the welcome provision), which by its meaning is what occurs at the first arrival, coming upon them in a state of heedlessness, and since they were being brought to the *ḥamīm* (scalding water) as camels are brought to water, and since His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿they will go around between it and scalding, boiling water﴾ [al-Rahman: 44] indicates that this is outside it, or outside its boiling mass, as the basins are in the enclosures, outside the places prepared for the camels, He said, making clear that they have something even more hideous than that, and hinting at it with the particle of delay: ﴿Then indeed their return﴾, that is, after their leaving their Zaqqum-hosting abode, ﴿is surely to the Blazing Fire﴾, that is, the one of intense blazing, sighing, weeping, and prolonged, lasting grief. Just as the party of God (*ḥizb Allah*) move about from the gardens of bliss to the gardens of refuge (*jannāt al-ma'wā*), for example, to the Gardens of Eden, to the Paradise of Firdaws, from which they do not desire any removal, just as the people of abundance and the great among the people of this world transfer their guests into continuous gardens and scenic spots, and entertain them in lofty palaces and villas.

(p-242)

When He had told of their punishment, which was caused by rigid adherence (judood) to habit that departs from the truth, and by clinging to what the soul has become accustomed to and what natures incline toward, derived from those whom they believed to be greater than themselves and more complete in intellect, He gave the reason for that, as a warning against the like of it, since it was the cause of the ruin of most of creation; and He emphasized it, because they deny the misguidance of those who established these customs for them. Those habits came from their fathers and others. So He said: ﴿Indeed, they found their fathers astray﴾; that is, they found them and took up what they became accustomed to; ﴿astray﴾; that is, deeply immersed in error. Therefore, what they are upon is clearly misguidance to anyone, which produces aversion toward its adherent.

﴿So they﴾; i.e., the distant, the hateful; ﴿upon their traces﴾; i.e., traces that are hardly clear to anyone, because their paths are obscure, because they are feeble, because of the extreme weakness of those paths, and because their landmarks have been effaced; not upon any others; ﴿are driven hastily﴾; i.e., as if some compeller were forcing them to hurry, so they are in the utmost haste toward it, without pausing for any proof or seeking illumination from any argument, (p-243) to the point that the one who hastens, because of the intensity of his pressing upon it, is seized by something like trembling. This is the opposite of their halting and rigidity regarding what our Messenger ﷺ brought them, concerning the tree of zaqqum and other matters, which are in the utmost clarity and manifestness. So they persisted in denying it and mocking it, and they insisted after the proofs had been established. Thus they were like mountains in firmness upon their misguidance, and like hard, heavy stones, fixed firmly in their clinging states.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 71:

When the Prophet (ﷺ) was intensely eager for their guidance, grieved over their straying, and distressed at their perversity and their destruction, and since straying, first in spite of reason and then, after the coming of the messengers, who are truthful, who bring miracles, and whose affairs compel one toward guidance, became almost inconceivable, He—glorified is He—consoled him with His words, by way of emphasis for the sake of greater affirmation: ﴿And certainly most of the earlier people had gone astray before them﴾; that is, before those he was calling, throughout all the time that preceded them; ﴿so that no generation passed after Adam (peace be upon him) without all of it, or most of it, being astray.﴾

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 72:

When it might be thought that it was because of the absence of messengers, He negated that with His words, emphasizing the like of this: ﴿And We had certainly sent﴾; that is, in accordance with the greatness that is Ours, which necessitates bringing clarity that leaves no doubt; ﴿among them warners﴾; that is, they warned them of the might of Allah, and made the best clarification clear to them. Yet despite that, misguidance overcame them, and the obstinacy of the people of truth against what is impossible, until Allah destroyed them by what He possesses of severe might; and this is the meaning of His saying:

(p-244) ﴿So look﴾: that is, as a consequence of the sending [of warners], consider what wonders We did in destroying them that deserve to be marvelled at and to serve as a warning against the like of them—by saying to whoever stayed behind them: look ﴿how﴾. And since that was a constant practice that never changed at all, He said: ﴿the end of those who were warned was﴾; that is, the final outcome of their affair, ﴿those who were warned﴾; that is, in that We destroyed them for their denial. So be patient through the hardships just as they were patient, and persist in calling with glad tidings and warning, until there comes to you the command of Allah.

When al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) says that the judgment of error upon the majority implies that the minority are not in their condition, he draws attention to the state of the obedient through his words, making an exception from the pronoun of "those warned" (al-mundharin): ﴿Except the servants of Allah﴾; that is: those whom He, glorified is He, chose for Himself by what He has of the attributes of perfection, so they deserved to be attributed to His Greatest Name; ﴿the sincere ones﴾; that is: those whom He made sincere for Himself, so they made their deeds sincere, not mixing into them any admixture for other than Him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 75:

Since the principal aim of the surah is tanzih (exalting God above all deficiencies), which means keeping far away from imperfections, the most fitting thing was for it to open with oaths by the angels, who are the purest of creation. The highest of creation is the one who strips his soul of worldly appetites through the striving, struggles and treatments that God bestows, until he attains to them and, together with his own virtue, passes beyond the lofty degrees of jihad. Therefore, the prophet most worthy of mention is the one who most stripped his soul of distractions, journeying toward his Master and ascending away from everything other than Him. The second father (p-245) was among the most worthy of this, because he stripped himself in jihad by calling to God for a thousand years, and then stripped himself of everything upon the surface of the water between earth and sky. So He (exalted) said, emphasizing what preceded it, namely that his long stay among his people, in calling them to God for so long, made it unlikely that they would agree with him, incline with him, and follow him; and because the conduct of the Arabs in denial, despite the successive miracles and continuous admonitions, was the conduct of one who denies that the messengers are granted victory and that the disbelievers are punished. This is an connective (ʿatf) upon what is implied: "The messengers endured hardships that no pages could contain, and they struggled against their peoples with their own selves and with supplication to God (exalted) concerning their affair": ﴿And Noah certainly called Us﴾, by reason of the greatness We possess; ﴿Noah﴾, by his saying: "My Lord, I am overcome, so help me," and similar words, which God related of him after great affairs that he suffered from them of distresses, hardships and calamities, so that We might remove from him what had exhausted him of their affair.

Since this sentence sufficed in place of explaining and lengthening the story, and since his supplication was followed by its answer, He said, using emphasis by the nominal sentence, the oath-indicating particle, the comprehensive particle for every praise, and the form of greatness, indicating that the horror of their punishment and the magnitude of their calamity reached such a degree that, despite its fame, it can scarcely be believed, so it requires great effort and intense attention. Thus the answer was the answer of one who does exactly that, even though (p-246) actions are, with respect to Him (glorified be He), of equal standing and require nothing but the mere will: ﴿So how excellent were the Answerers﴾; that is, We were, by the greatness We possess, the excellent answerers to him and to others among those who were excellent answerers to Us. This is Our attribute, and it admits of no change.

Since the meaning of this was: We answered him with an answer that is the utmost in deserving praise, in bringing him to his aim, in carrying him, and carrying those who believed in him, and in taking vengeance on those who denied him, as is always our custom, He followed it with His saying: ﴿And We delivered him﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness; ﴿and his family﴾, that is, those who agreed with him in the religion; ﴿from the great distress﴾, which is the harm of drowning.

The commentary is on surah 37, verse 77.

﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾; that is, exclusively; ﴿the survivors﴾. Because all the people of the earth drowned, so that no one at all remained from them; and of the people of the Ark, none had offspring except his children. So We perpetuated him in his purity, making him the second father. Thus the Arabs and the non-Arabs (ʿAjam) are the children of Sam; the Sudanese are the children of Ham; and the Turks, the Saqaliba (Slavs), Yajuj and Majuj (Gog and Magog) are the children of Yafith. Therefore, whoever follows his practice in goodness, he has a like reward for it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 78:

When he mentioned that He blessed his offspring, he made known that He perpetuated his remembrance with goodness among his people, so He said: ﴿And We left for him﴾; that is, a good praise. But He omitted the object (maf'ul) and made the verb intransitive (lazim), so the meaning becomes: We caused to fall upon him the leaving (of a good remembrance) by something that is of his greatness and the goodness of his remembrance, to such an extent that its description is rare; ﴿among the later generations﴾; that is, everyone who came after his time until the Day of Religion.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 79:

Since God had decreed from eternity that he (Noah) would be safe from every harm, despite the great number of his enemies, his long stay among them, and the severity of their opposition, God (exalted is He) said, as a new and laudatory statement: ﴿Peace﴾, that is, great peace, ﴿upon Noah﴾, from every living being, from the jinn, mankind and the angels, because of God's peace upon him.

Since the language of all the people of the earth in his time was one language, and they were all his people, and there was no prophet in his time, his prophethood was the pivot of the circle of that age, and his message was general to his people, while the other created beings were followers of them, God singled him out in the greeting by saying: ﴿in the worlds﴾, that is, he is mentioned among all of them, both verbally and in meaning, and he is greeted continually until the Hour arrives. The distinctiveness of our Prophet (ﷺ) is that he was sent to all creation, despite the difference of tongues, and despite the continuance of his message forever and ever, and the fact that his law abrogates other laws without being abrogated, and the fact that all creation will be under his banner on the Day of Resurrection. There the full extent of what he was granted of the universality of his mission will become manifest, in addition to what became manifest of it in this world.

Since the sense was: "We did this to him because of his good-doing; and the misguided used to deny that the callers to God and their followers would be saved from among them," he informed, in the context of emphasis, that He does to every doer of good what He did to him. So He said: ﴿Indeed We﴾; that is, despite Our greatness; ﴿thus﴾ (p-248) that is, the like of that recompense: with a good mention and deliverance from every evil; ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾; that is, those who strip themselves of the darkness of the soul, toward the angelic lights, such that they never neglect the One who is worshipped, and never part from witnessing (the Divine) for an instant.

When this sentence had necessarily conveyed his (Abraham's) good treatment of the one who does good, he gave the reason for what it had conveyed with his words, emphasizing it (to show his attentiveness to him, by reminding him of what he desires, and to refute those who denied him): ﴿Indeed he is among Our servants﴾; that is, those who are fit for Us to attribute them to the station of Our greatness; ﴿the believers﴾; that is, those firmly established in this attribute and rooted in it. Thus it is known that faith is the ultimate aim from man, because He gave the reason for the rescue by (his) good deeds, and (his) good deeds by (his) clear statement.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 82:

When the restriction of his descendants to survival had implied the destruction of others, he (God) led with what deserves praise of him, out of concern for it and to encourage the like of it. He then reported regarding his enemies that He had struck them, because they had not adorned themselves with what had been the cause of his happiness, namely faith. He said, pointing to the greatness which He, glory be to Him, brought into being in their drowning, with the particle of delay: ﴿Then We drowned﴾, that is, by that greatness of Ours which nothing can withstand, ﴿the others﴾, that is, those who opposed him in their sayings and actions, so they deserved the opposite of what We did with him. They were all the people of the earth, other than the people of the Ark. All of them (p-249) were his people, as is apparent from the verses when their expression about the call, the drowning, and his - peace be upon him - supplication against them is carefully considered, and as is apparent from what the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others narrated from Anas - may Allah be pleased with him - in the hadith of intercession, that people will say: "Go to Nuh, the first prophet whom Allah sent to the people of the earth." They were only a people, no more, because they were of one tongue before the confusion of tongues, by the agreement of the historians. This is like the Arabs, who are all called a people, despite their spread and the breadth of their lands, because they are united in language, although they are tribes that cannot be counted and are not joined by one lineage, except that they all trace back to Isma'il - peace be upon him - and it has been said: to what is above him. The genealogists agreed that Adnan is of the descendants of Isma'il - peace be upon him - and they said: he is of the descendants of Adnan. They differed about Qahtan, the father of Yemen, and likewise Thaqif. It was said: both of them are of the descendants of Isma'il - peace be upon him - and it was said: no. Then whoever said that Thaqif are of the descendants of Isma'il - peace be upon him - said: he is of the descendants of Adnan, and some of them said: no. Then among the descendants of Adnan are Rabi'a and Mudar, and below Mudar are Kinana, Hudhayl, al-Qarra, Khuza'a, Asad, Tamim, Muzayna, al-Rabab, Dabba, and Qays. Below that are Bahila, Ashja', Fazara, Kinana, Quraysh, and many others. Below Rabi'a is Bakr ibn Wa'il and others. Below that are Shayban, Abd al-Qays, and al-Namir, and many others. Below Qahtan, the father of Yemen, are Lakhm, Judham, Amila, Ghassan, Kinda, Hamdan, al-Azd, and among them the Ansar, and many others besides. (p-250) All of these, despite this branching, spreading, and difference in religions, and even in some dialects, are called "one nation" and "a people," because their tongue is united in the origin of the Arabic language. The children of Ishaq are not among them, by agreement, although they are the sons of their paternal uncle, because they differ from them in language. Moreover, they are closer in lineage to Qahtan and Thaqif according to the one who said that they (the Arabs) are not of the descendants of Isma'il - peace be upon him. Likewise, the children of Ishaq - peace be upon him - split by the split of language. So the children of Isma'il are a people, the children of Esau, who are the Romans, are a people, and likewise all other nations: only language distinguishes between them. The generality of his call to the children of Adam - peace be upon him - in this sense does not detract from the particularity of our Prophet ﷺ, through the generality of the call and the sending to others than his people. As for generality, he was sent to every being among humankind, angels, and jinn. As for calling peoples, what is meant is that he was sent to those who share his language and to those who differ from it. As for others, he was not sent to those who differ from him in language, nor to beings other than his kind, although it is recommended for him that he command and forbid those who differ in language, as a matter of enjoining good and forbidding evil, not as an obligation. Even if we grant concerning Nuh - peace be upon him - that he was not sent to all the people of the earth, it is refuted by Adam - peace be upon him - for he was a sent prophet, as Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Abi Umar, Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba, al-Harith (p-251) ibn Abi Usama, Abu Ya'la al-Mawsili, and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh narrated in their Musnads, and al-Tabarani in his al-Mu'jam al-Awsat, from Abu Umama al-Bahili and Abu Dharr - may Allah be pleased with them both - and in some chains of Abu Dharr there is explicit mention of his being sent. No one doubts that he was a messenger to all whom his descendants reached, and they are all the people of the earth. Likewise Nuh - peace be upon him - no one doubts that after the drowning he was a messenger to all the people of the Ark, as he had been before that, and they are all the people of the earth. Therefore, what I have presented, that the particularity of being sent is to those of differing tongues from all the children of Adam, and to those who differ in kind from every creature, is what removes the difficulty. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 83:

Since Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had such detachment from human attributes and soul-bound attachments, and such elevation to angelic states, as was not possessed by any of the prophets who came before or after him, namely: his open opposition to his people; his proclamation, in that opposition, of the breaking of the idols; his exposure of the doctrine of disbelief; his standing alone, apart from all besides Allah, amid the blazing fires; his self-effacement, by heart and tongue, from all created beings; then his migration from his homeland; then his separation from loved ones and brethren, by placing his firstborn son and his concubine in that place where there is neither human nor jinn; then his undertaking to sacrifice his son with the utmost strength and the firmest resolve; then his building of the House with its foundations, as a qibla for those who are detached from the believers, in every time, from all save the Sovereign, the Judge, who form ranks at every prayer like the ranks of the noble angels; and since he was in agreement with Nuh (peace be upon him), together with the blessing that had preceded in his progeny, such that they now number nearly half the people of the earth; and since the most famous of his affairs was in fire, which is the opposite of the most famous of Nuh's affairs, in water; [Allah] followed it with him, saying, emphasizing, also to show the nobility and the lofty station he possessed in leadership, which calls for eagerness in praising him, alerting to what befits completing resolve in following him, and refuting those who claimed that he innovated and departed from those who came before him: ﴿And indeed, of his party﴾, that is, those whose secret mingled with his secret and whose affair agreed with his affair, in firmness in religion and in patient endurance against the corrupters; ﴿was Ibrahim﴾;

Then he linked it to the meaning of "following" (al-mushayaʿa), as an explanation of what the following consisted in. His statement, supposing a questioner who asks, "When did he follow him?": ﴿when﴾, that is, at the time when; ﴿he came to his Lord﴾, that is, the one who had done well in raising him; ﴿with a sound heart﴾, that is, one completely free of love for anything other than Him. The "coming" is a metaphor for sincerity (ikhlas) that has no admixture in it, just as one who comes to you has no part of his body with anyone else.

Then He substituted for that what is evidence of it, saying: ﴿When he said to his father﴾; that is, the one who was the greatest of people in his regard, the most esteemed in his eyes, and the most honored by him; ﴿and to his people﴾; that is, those who possessed such strength and fortune that lions fear them; ﴿What is it that you worship?﴾; that is, what is it that ﴿you worship﴾, belittling their affair and the affair of what they worship, alerting that in reality there is no cause for them that would compel them to worship these, while being unconcerned with their multitude, not fearful of their power, and not heedful of the inclination of human nature toward their affection.

When he had hinted to them at denial, he stated it openly, saying, placing the object first for emphasis of restriction: ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than Allah that you desire?﴾ That is, a turning of the truth away from its face to its back. Since he made their objects of worship the very essence of falsehood, he substituted for it his saying ﴿gods﴾, then he belittled their state by his saying ﴿other than Allah﴾, that is, the One who has no equal; ﴿you desire﴾.

Since the witnessing (shuhud) had already overwhelmed him in his belittling of them, he thereby made a great threat concerning their act, saying, pointing out that the thought of ruin (ʿatab) is enough to deter the intelligent person from prohibition: ﴿So what is your thought?﴾ And since ingratitude for favor (kufran al-ihsan) is severe, he reminded them of His favor, preserving the context of the threat, by alluding that the fear of the cutting off of favor is enough in that regard. So he said: ﴿concerning the Lord of the worlds﴾; that is: the One who is singular in creating all the substances (jawahir) and accidents (aʿrad), and in nurturing them. Therefore He deserves their singling Him out in worship. Do you suppose that He will not punish you, when you have turned the blessings He bestowed upon you toward the worship of other than Him? This is an allusion to denying that the like of this is permissible, and that it is certain that a benefactor does not approve of the continuation of the flow of his favor to one who attributes him to another.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 88:

When the context made clear the intensity of his (ﷺ) enmity with them, and God (Exalted) had established His custom of placing in the stars indications of some speculative matters, especially the (al-bahrānāt) concerning the kinds of illnesses; and the people of that land, (p-254) namely the Kasdaniyyun (Chaldeans), as has preceded in al-An'am, and as Ibn 'Abbas - may Allah be pleased with him and his father - said, and as the books of the conquests indicate, were among the most intent of people in observing the stars and in inferring from them the conditions of this world, regarding some of what had occurred and some of what would occur; and he (ﷺ) wanted to stay behind from going with them to the place where they gathered for the festival, in order to break the idols, and he wanted to conceal from them the time of the breaking so that he could accomplish that; God (Exalted) said, relating about him, indicating by its being a consequence of what preceded: ﴿So he glanced a glance﴾; that is, one glance; ﴿at the stars﴾; when they asked him to come out with them to their festival, so that they would not deny his staying behind from them; giving them the impression that he had inferred from that glance an inner sickness that would befall him; for they might have denied his being ill if he had informed them without looking at the stars, since the health was evident in him.

﴿Then he said﴾: i.e., immediately after this glance, giving the impression that it was its cause. Since his body was healthy, and he was therefore liable to have his report doubted, he emphasized it and said: ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾. Thus he gave the impression that his meaning was bodily illness, though he intended that his heart was sick because of their gods, his thought divided concerning their affair, because he intended a great matter, which was breaking them. The root "سَقَمَ" (saqama), with its five permutations, "سَقَمَ", "سَمَقَ", "قَسَمَ", "قَمَسَ", and "مَقَسَ", revolves around division (qasm). Thus "al-saqam" (السَّقامُ), like "saḥāb" (cloud), "jabal" (mountain), and "qufl" (lock), means illness, i.e., (p-255) because it divides strength and thought. Ibn al-Qattā' said: "سَقِمَ": illness prolonged with him; "قَسَّمَهُ": divided it into parts; "الدَّهْرُ القَوْمَ": time separated the people; "al-qism" (القِسْمُ), with a kasra (the vowel "i", a short vowel mark), means a share; "al-qasm" (القَسْمُ), with a fatha (the vowel "a"), means a gift, and it has no plural; also: opinion, doubt, defect, water, decree, character, and custom; both are pronounced with a kasra. The notion of separation is evident in all of these: as for gift, it divides and distributes wealth; opinion divides thought; doubt likewise; defect divides one's honor; water is the most easily divided of things; decree separates its owner from others; and likewise character and custom. "Al-muqassam" (المُقَسَّمُ), like "mu'aẓẓam", means one who is preoccupied, because his thought is scattered; and also the beautiful, because one divides speech in describing him. "Al-qasam" (القَسَمُ), with fatha, means an oath by God. "Qad aqsama" (قَدْ أقْسَمَ), i.e., he removed the division of thought. "Al-qasāmah" (القَسامَةُ) means beauty, because it distributes the viewer's thought; the perfume-seller's jar is likewise, for the goodness of its scent. "Al-qasām" (القَسامُ), like "saḥāb", means intensity of heat, because it disturbs thought so that it divides it; or it is the beginning of the midday hour; or the time of the sun's zenith, when the sun is at its finest as a mirror, so thought is divided upon it for its beauty at that time, and for what occurs upon it afterward. "Al-qams" (القَمْسُ) means diving, because the diver divides the water by his dive. "Al-qams" also means the agitation of the fetus in the womb, because it divides thought and almost divides the belly by its agitation. "Al-qāmūs" (القامُوسُ) means the greater part of the sea, because the sea divided the land, and its greater part is more worthy of this name. "Al-qawāmis" (القَوامِسُ) means calamities, because they divide thought. "Inqamasa al-najm" (انْقَمَسَ النَّجْمُ) means the star set, i.e., it took its share of setting as it had taken its share of rising, or it removed division by its motion. "Maqasahu fī al-mā'" (مَقَسَهُ في الماءِ) means he plunged it, so the water divided by his immersing it in it. "Al-qirba" (القِرْبَةَ): he filled it; so he placed in it water that is easy to divide, and his taking the water he placed in it is a division of the water taken from it. "Maqasa al-shay'" (مَقَسَ الشَّيْءَ) means he broke it. "Al-mā'" (الماءُ): it flowed, so it was divided; and he divided the land. "Huwa yamqusu al-shi'r kayfa shā'" (هُوَ يَمْقُسُ الشِّعْرَ كَيْفَ شاءَ): i.e., he composes it, dividing it from the rest of speech as he wills. "Al-tamqīs fī al-mā'" (التَّقْمِيسُ في الماءِ) means pouring much of it, for that is dividing it. "Samaqa sumūqan" (سَمَقَ سُمُوقًا) means he rose high and grew tall, so that by his height he accepts division that what is lower than him does not accept.

When they had understood from him the apparent meaning of his words, and suspected in him what appeared from his condition, but his greatness in their eyes left them no room except submission, they left him. Then He (Exalted) said, making it a consequence of their words and indicating their deeming his illness unlikely through the form of tafa'ala (the reflexive/effortful verb pattern): ﴿So they turned away﴾; that is, they exerted themselves and compelled themselves to depart, ﴿from him﴾, toward the place of their gathering and the observance of their festival. He emphasized the meaning and made it explicit by saying: ﴿turning their backs﴾; that is, toward their place of worship. Thus the time was clear for him, free from any watcher.

Then he turned aside stealthily to their gods, with nimbleness, lightness, vigor and resolve; al-Baydawi said: its origin is inclining by means of a stratagem. [He went] to their gods, that is, their idols which they claimed to be gods, and they had placed food before them. He addressed them as one addresses someone who understands, because of their placing them thereby among those who understand. He said, denouncing them, (p-257) mocking them outwardly and rebuking his people in reality: "Will you not eat?"

Then he increased in making the truth manifest and in mocking their (the idols') lowliness from the rank of their worshippers; so he said: ﴿What is (the matter)﴾; i.e., what has befallen ﴿you﴾; that ﴿you do not speak﴾?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 93:

When (Exalted is He) informed that He had manifested what he knew inwardly of the proof, He said: ﴿Then he turned﴾; that is, as a consequence of his establishing the proof, he came upon them in a superior manner, ﴿upon them﴾, with the utmost vigor, agility and nimbleness, striking them, ﴿striking them with the right hand﴾; that is, with the utmost force. And the construction placed the verbal noun (maṣdar) to indicate the strength of his resolve, such that all of it became striking.

Since their knowing of the breaking of the idols led them to suspect him, because of what they had been hearing from him of disparagement of them and his oath that he would surely scheme against them, they came to him. He reported this by saying, as a consequence: ﴿Then they came hastening towards him﴾; and he indicated that it was from a distant place by his saying: ﴿hastening towards him﴾; that is, they hurried. The reading of Hamzah, with the passive form (yuzaffūn, "they are driven"), is more indicative of the intensity of the hastening, because it indicates that they came in a state as if a bearer was carrying them along in it to hasten, and a compeller was forcing them to it, due to the intensity of the grief that was in their souls.

Since it was known that they had spoken to him about this, and their speech was long, and the soul's eagerness for his reply was greater, he resumed the report about him with His words: ﴿He said﴾, not fearing them and not concerned with them, because he saw them as perishing, rebuking them: ﴿Do you worship﴾. He called them with the present tense to repentance and return to God, and he expressed it with the particle for that which does not reason, as is the truth, so he said: ﴿what you carve﴾. That is: if worship were due to anyone other than God, then they would be more worthy that you worship them, because you made them, and they did not make you.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 96:

When the One who alone bestows blessing, and who alone deserves worship, was in question; and when creation (al-iijad) is among the greatest of blessings; and since He had made clear that they only worshipped them (the idols) on account of their own work which they had made in them, and so He transformed them into the shape they took; He said (exalted is He), explaining that He alone is their Creator, and the Creator of their deeds, for which they in reality worshipped nothing but these, and that their carved idols have no place in creation, and therefore no place in worship: ﴿And Allah created you﴾; that is, while the fact is that the Greatest King, to whom none is equal, ﴿created you﴾; that is, brought you into existence in these forms; ﴿and what you make﴾; that is, and created your work and what you make. So He alone is the One who originates all creation, of essences and of attributes. And it is well known that none is worshipped except one who is like this, because it is not permissible for any rational person to give thanks for a blessing except to its Lord.

Since the listener knows that they would necessarily not answer him with anything, and so he yearns for that, he is answered with His saying: ﴿They said, "Build for him a structure"﴾; that is, for his sake; ﴿a structure﴾; that is, of firewood; until it becomes like a great mountain; then set it alight until its blaze intensifies greatly, so that it becomes a blazing furnace (jahim); ﴿then throw him into the blazing furnace﴾; that is, into the middle of that fire; and it is at its most intense state of kindling.

Since this was a consequence of their intent to humiliate him, He said: ﴿So they intended a scheme against him﴾; that is, against Ibrahim (peace be upon him), by means of what they had done; ﴿a scheme﴾; that is, a plan (tadbir) aimed at nullifying his affair, so that their affair would prevail and their religion would not be nullified by the incapacity they had displayed. ﴿So We made them﴾; that is, by Our might, as a consequence of their action; ﴿the lowest﴾; the vanquished, by what We nullified of their fire. We made it for him ﴿coolness and safety﴾; in contrast to its usual nature in action; so Our action was carried out, and this was beyond the normal course of custom (kharq lil-'adah). Their action, which was according to the requirement of custom, was nullified; thus their incapacity became evident in their deed, just as their incapacity had become evident in their speech, through the proof We had displayed on the tongue of Our intimate friend (peace be upon him); and Our power and Our will became manifest. I have explained the kayd (scheme) by what I have mentioned because it means deceit, wickedness, stratagem, trickery, and planning, whether in truth or in falsehood, and war and fear; all these meanings, as you see, revolve around planning, the employment of thought, and the management of opinion.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 99:

When the implied sense was: "So he resolved to leave their land, because they had turned away from proof to obstinacy," He joined to it His saying: ﴿And he said﴾; that is, Abraham, peace be upon him, to the one who would perceive in him that his words would give life to him from the death of ignorance; emphasizing, because a person's separation from his homeland is hardly believed: ﴿Indeed, I am going﴾; that is, emigrating without hesitation. They said: he was the first of creation to emigrate. ﴿To my Lord﴾; that is, to the place to which the Benefactor commanded me to migrate; so no one will restrict me in my worship there.

When the state of the one hearing him was worthy of his saying: Who will give you knowledge of what achieves this purpose of yours, from identifying the place and what you will do there that would bring about the good, and what you will do to reach it? He said: ﴿He will guide me﴾; that is, to all of that, with a promise that admits no breaking; to everything in it that is a upbringing for me in the matter of the emigration, because He commanded me with it; and He does not command something except that He sets up for it a sign that guides to it, and makes easy for His seeker who strives in his affair the path to it. The expressions have differed concerning the journey of the chosen ones toward the holy presences. So this expression refers to the matter of the Friend (Khalil), peace be upon him; and He expressed the matter of the Interlocutor (Kalim), peace be upon him, by His saying: ﴿And when Moses came at Our appointed time﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]; and the matter of the Beloved, peace be upon him, by His saying: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. Al-Ustadh Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri said, distinguishing between these stations: Abraham, peace be upon him, was in the eye of separation (al-farq), meaning that after what he had been in of unification (al-jam') when he broke the idols, from annihilation (fana') from all other than Allah, he returned to the state of separation, because that is necessary; and Moses, peace be upon him, was in the eye of unification (al-jam'), because He reported his action without attributing to him a saying; then He reported that he said: "My Lord, show me," so he did not see other than Him, glory be to Him, so he sought that He show Himself; and this is annihilation. Our Prophet ﷺ was in the eye of the unification of unification, because no saying or action was attributed to him; rather he was the one intended; up to His saying: ﴿That We may show him of Our signs﴾ [al-Isra': 1]; this is annihilation even from annihilation. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Isra': 1], so He affirmed for him, along with that, perfection.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 100:

When he (Abraham) did not find anyone to help him in emigrating (al-hijrah) except Lot, the son of his brother, peace be upon them both, he said, calling out in the manner of intimate servants by dropping the particle (of address): ﴿My Lord﴾; that is, O You who are good to me; ﴿grant me [a child] from﴾; that is, a son from ﴿the righteous﴾. He omitted the noun it qualifies, because the word "grant" (hibah) had become predominantly used for a son. Thus, as a consequence of his supplication, We responded to it for him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 101:

﴿So We gave him good news of a boy﴾; i.e., a male of utmost strength, from whom youthful vigor (al-ghilma) arises.

Since this description may suggest levity (al-taysh), He described him with what preserves his purity and removes any turbidity from it, saying: ﴿forbearing﴾; i.e., he does not hasten to punish when he has the power to do so, because he is at the utmost in gravity and steadfastness. This points to his being subjected to some trial through which it becomes clear that he is the offspring of his father, of whom it is said: "Indeed Abraham was forbearing" (halim). Forbearance (al-hilm) exists only after knowledge ('ilm), and the firm establishment of knowledge is the cause of the existence of forbearance; it is the breadth of the chest toward the faults of creation and the lowness of their characters.

This boy is undoubtedly Isma'il, peace be upon him, for several reasons. Among them is his being described as forbearing, while Isaac, peace be upon him, is described in Surat al-Hijr as knowing (alim). Among them also is that this supplication was made at the time of the emigration (al-hijra), when he was a youth hoping for a son; he was his firstborn, who was born to him through this good news. He is the one who was in Mecca, the place of the sacrifice, so the acts of his sacrifice became rites (manasik) of the Hajj at Mina, just as the acts of his mother in the blessed city of Mecca at the beginning of her affair, when she was about to die of thirst, became rites and landmarks there. As for Isaac, peace be upon him, the good news came to him suddenly while he was not hoping for a son, because of his old age and his wife's despair; for this reason he questioned the matter. It is not reported that he was separated from his mother in Bayt al-Maqdis. Had he been the one sacrificed, the Prophet ﷺ would have mentioned him by this description when he was asked about the most noble (al-akram), and he said: "Yusuf is the prophet of Allah, son of the prophet of Allah, son of the prophet of Allah, son of the beloved friend of Allah." The narration that alludes to his being the one sacrificed is weak; indeed, our shaykh Ibn Hajar stated in his takhrij of the hadiths of the Kashshaf that its chain contains fabricators (wudda').

Moreover, this surah is the surah of exaltation (al-tanzih), so the most deserving of mention in it, as has passed, is the one most deeply rooted in ancient stripping away (al-tajrid) of the self; and he is the most worthy of that from the time he was an infant until his sacrifice was treated. He is not mentioned openly. Had the intended meaning of this statement not been him, then in this surah, whose subject is this, the one most firmly established in the intended description would have been omitted. That would be outside the path of eloquence (nahj al-balagha), which is the matching of speech to what the situation requires (mutabaqat al-maqal li-muqtada al-hal). Rather, this situation does not require mentioning Isaac, peace be upon him, because no agreed-upon stripping away (tajrid) is known for him. His mention came only to explain the recompense of Abraham, peace be upon him, for what his station required of him in excellence, in the domain of stripping away and annihilation (al-fana'). And Allah is the Granter of success.

(p-263) Since the good news from God never fails, the implied meaning is: "So he was given a boy, as We said." ﴿So when he reached﴾ the age of striving, being with him, ﴿with him﴾ — that is, with his father specifically, and accompanying him — ﴿the striving﴾, which the father approves of, and in which he prepares his soul regarding the child and trusts him, and which is not tied to a limit; for it requires that both of them reach the limit of striving together. There is no sense of this in regard to Ibrahim (peace be upon him), nor in regard to striving, because the complement of the verbal noun (maṣdar) does not precede it; and if it were placed after it, it would not convey the restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ) that indicates his young age, which conveys the information that he would reach, in that matter with him, what he would not reach with anyone else, due to the great compassion of the father and the firm affection of the son, which obliges obedience to him. The scholars differed in estimating that by age: some of them said thirteen years, and some said seven years. Therefore He restricted it to the father, because others do not feel compassion for the child, so they would burden him with what is beyond his capacity, and he had not reached the full extent of striving. ﴿He said﴾ — that is, Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿O my son﴾, addressing him with a form of tenderness, compassion and endearment, recounting to him with the present tense the state in which he saw him, and depicting it for him — not for the repetition of the vision, for he does not need repetition, nor to deliberate; for God (Exalted) showed him the dominion of the heavens and the earth — and he emphasized it, because of what is in human nature of deeming it impossible that such a thing be said in its reality, and to inform him that it was a dream of revelation, not confused dreams. (p-264) ﴿Indeed I see in the dream﴾ — that is, and you know that the visions of the prophets are revelation — ﴿that I am slaughtering you﴾ — that is, I am attempting to slaughter you while awake, by a command from God (Exalted); and for this reason it was as he said; and had he expressed it in the past tense, it would have passed and been completed. It was in a dream that this matter of great gravity occurred, so that the certainty of the prophets (peace be upon them) in what comes to them from God in every state might be known.

When the prophets (peace be upon them) were the most compassionate of people and the most sincere in counsel, he wished to see what was in his son's mind; so if it was in accordance with what he loved, he would be pleased and make him firm; and otherwise he would strive to bring him to what he loved, so that he would face the trial while it is easier for him, and that would be greater for his reward, due to the completeness of his submission; and so that consultation would become a sunnah, for indeed "no one who consults regrets." On account of that he said: ﴿So look﴾ — with the eye of your insight — ﴿what﴾ — that is, what it is that — ﴿you see﴾ — that is, in this vision. So it was a test of his patience, not a consultation for him. ﴿He said﴾, confirming God's praise of him for forbearance: ﴿O my father﴾, showing courtesy toward him with what indicates veneration and reverence: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾ — that is, everything for which a command has come to you from God (Exalted), and for which a command from Him — glory be to Him — is renewed for you; for I do not accuse you of lacking compassion or of poor judgment, nor do I accuse God in His decree. The narrative is evidence of the occurrence of a command with what is impossible for other than it, and of most of the commands from Him; and this has been mentioned earlier in al-Baqarah, at His words: "Whether you warn them or do not warn them."

(p-265) When he knew his obedience, the listener longed for his submission and patience, so He resumed his words: ﴿You will find me﴾ — that is, with a firm promise, without any hesitation, truthful, as God (Exalted) informed about him, without any failing in it; and he was truthful in promise.

Since it is among the characteristics of the perfected that they do not make definite statements about future matters, because they know the power of God (Exalted) to annul resolutions by coming between a person and his heart, he said: ﴿If God wills﴾ — that is, He who is singled out with encompassing the attributes of perfection; and he emphasized his promise with this matter, which such a thing hardly seems to be believed, by his words: ﴿among the patient﴾ — that is, those who are foremost in patience, reaching its utmost limit. This is among the greatest of what is meant by His words: ﴿He was truthful in promise﴾ [Maryam: 54].

"Even if I were given poison by the hand of the beloved, the poison would be sweet from his hand."

He made this great matter, in the dream, a sign of the truthfulness of the states of the prophets, asleep and awake, and of the truthfulness of their resolutions, and of their submission to all commands in all states. It is narrated that Satan whispered to him about slaughtering him, so he recognized him and threw at him seven pebbles; and that became a law regarding the stoning at the Jamarat. Among the most subtle aspects of this is that when they were at the height of detachment from the ties of preoccupations, their actions were made into rites and laws for the worship of Hajj, whose spirit is detachment for coming forth to God (Exalted).

When Abraham was assured of him, he hastened to do what he had been commanded, and by using the particle fa' he indicated how close his time was to the time of this statement, so He said: ﴿So when they had both submitted﴾; that is, they both cast themselves, in deed, in utmost sincerity at the moment of carrying it out, with all their strength, into the hand of the command, and neither of them had any reluctance, refusal, or inner conflict in any part of that.

﴿And he flung him down upon his forehead﴾; that is, Ibrahim, peace be upon them both, threw him down, a good and swift throwing, with complete contentment on his part and full compliance from Isma'il, peace be upon him. He indicated the swiftness by the lam (li-) placed in the position of "ʿalā" (on), so He said: ﴿for the jabin﴾; that is, one of the two sides of the forehead. It is the posture of laying down what is to be slaughtered. This comes from their saying "tallahu," meaning he threw him down; and from it the word "tall" (a mound of earth) is named; and "talalta fulanan fi yadika" means you pushed him down gently. As for al-jabin, al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: it is above the temple (ṣudgh), and they are two jabin, one on the right side of the forehead and one on its left.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 104:

Since it is clear that the implied sense is: "The answer: when he (Abraham) undertook to slaughter him with a resolve sharper than the spear, and a heart in its steadfastness of the utmost firmness, We prevented the blade from taking effect by Our power, and We turned back its sharp edge from his tender neck by Our hands and Our might," He joined to it His saying: ﴿And We called out to him﴾; and He magnified this calling by the particle of explanation (an-, "that"), so He said: ﴿That, O Abraham﴾;

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 105:

When the place of expectation was praise for him, he said: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾; that is, a great fulfilment; ﴿the vision﴾ regarding your slaughtering him. For you have indeed striven at that and exerted your utmost effort in it, and you did what you saw in the dream. So he was not slaughtered, because you did not see that you had slaughtered him. So refrain from pursuing the slaughter beyond this. And since the implied sense was: "We rewarded you for that, for your excellence, beyond what you loved, and We made you an imam (leader) for the God-fearing, and We granted you a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations, and We made your family the chosen ones, and We filled the two horizons with them," he gave the reason for this, namely that this is His custom always, in the past and in the present, and so he said what follows.

When he (ﷺ) was in the resolve and determination to slaughter, that resolve was one whose rank the Pleiades and Arcturus fall short of, and that determination was one whose lofty station and exalted greatness the high spheres fall short of, it would not settle from its surging nor cool from its boiling and seething except by a severe command and an emphatic, decisive word, he said, emphasizing, to alert that his resolve had reached a limit of this kind, and that carrying out the command is easier than restraining oneself after having actually begun, by means of a prohibition: ﴿Indeed, thus﴾; that is, like this great reward; ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾.

Since his reward was exceedingly great, its greatness was indicated by giving the reason for his honoring with it, by saying, in a manner that is wondrous and magnifying, emphatically, as an alert that it breaks the usual custom: ﴿Indeed, this﴾; i.e., the command and the obedience in it; ﴿is indeed the trial﴾; i.e., the testing that exposes whatever is mixed with it, whatever it may be; ﴿the manifest﴾; i.e., clearly evident in its own kind, very much so, making plain to the beholder that it is a trial.

Since He had first mentioned what was more important than his prohibition against treating him (the son) and the good news of the reward, He mentioned the ransoming of him by means of that which He made a lasting tradition, by which he is remembered with honor throughout the passing of days and the succession of years. And since the one ransomed is the one in whose hand the captive is, and Isma'il was in the hand of Ibrahim, peace be upon them both, while he was in the process of destroying him, the Exalted (ta'ala) made Himself, the Sanctified, the Ransomer (fadin), because the fadin is the one who gives the ransom (fida'), which is what is paid for the release (fakak) of the captive. And He made Ibrahim, peace be upon him, the one ransomed (muftada minhu), as an honoring of him, although in reality he was like an instrument that has no action of its own. Allah (ta'ala) is in truth the one from whom the ransom is taken. So He said: ﴿And We ransomed him﴾, i.e., the sacrificed one, from carrying out his slaughter and completing it, as an honoring of him; ﴿with a great sacrifice﴾ (dhibh), i.e., with that which ought to be slaughtered and be suitable as a thing to be slaughtered, and it is a ram from Paradise. It is said that it is the one which Habil offered, so Allah accepted it from him. ﴿Great﴾ (azim), i.e., in its body, its measure, and its rank, because it was accepted, and made a precedent (mustann bihi), and made a religious practice (dinan) until the end of time.

Since He, glory be to Him, when He bestows a favour, makes known that it is great; so when He mentions the act and leaves out the object, He intends its magnificence and greatness. He said: ﴿And We left upon him﴾; that is, upon the one who was sacrificed, something whose beauty is such that its description would be long. And since it was of a kind that is not forgotten, He said: ﴿among later generations﴾. Of this kind of omission is what preceded regarding his description as one "true to the promise," for he promised to be patient in the face of the slaughter, and he was true to it.

When He had glorified the boy, He went on to glorify his father, with a statement that, along with honouring him, indicates his safety: ﴿Peace be upon Abraham﴾; that is: safety is for him, and for his son; and greeting, and salutation, and honour in both abodes.

Since this address is to those who came after him, peace be upon him, and they are all beloved, honored, exalted and dignified, there was no circumstance requiring emphasis. So He said: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like this great reward, ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾, without mentioning "inna" (indeed), the emphatic particle.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 111:

Since all the religious communities (milal) are unanimously agreed upon his love, and all of them claim to follow him and to have the rank of nearness to him, He said, giving the reason for his reward by this praise, in the context of emphasis, coaxing them to follow him in faith, and rebuking those who deny that faith necessitates goodness:

﴿Indeed, he was among Our servants, the believers.﴾ That is, those who deserve the attribution of servitude and worship to Us. So let no one who is stripped of faith hope for the rank of following him. Al-Razi said: True absolute faith is witnessing God's majesty and His oneness, finding tranquility in Him in every loved and disliked matter, leaving one's own will to His will, and submitting to His command in all conditions.

When He had completed his story concerning the matter of the one to be sacrificed,

Al-Biqa'i began to mention what Allah rewarded him with for that. He made from it the matter of Ishaq, peace be upon him. So He said: ﴿And We gave him good tidings﴾, i.e., as a reward for his patience in hastening to carry out the command to sacrifice Isma'il, peace be upon him: ﴿of Ishaq﴾, born; as an addition to him, after We had let Isma'il, peace be upon him, go free; while he was ﴿a prophet﴾, i.e., in Our decree, or by his existence, his prophethood having been predestined. And since this word may be applied to one who claims prophethood falsely (al-mutanabbi, the self-declared prophet), he removed the problem of this possibility, though it is weak, by His saying: ﴿of the righteous﴾, i.e., those who have attained the highest rank of righteousness, so that it encompasses most of the righteous attributes.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 113 (part 1 of 2):

When He had praised Ibrahim (peace be upon him) for what he went through, which no one else had experienced in the same way, and since one of the greatest rewards a person can receive is blessing in his descendants, He said: ﴿And We blessed him﴾; that is, blessed the forbearing boy, who is the sacrificed one (al-dhabih) referred to in this narration, the one about whom this whole discourse was initiated. The last pronoun that clearly referred back to him was the "ha'" (his) in ﴿And We ransomed him﴾ [al-Saffat: 107], and then in ﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾ [al-Saffat: 108]. In my view, this is preferable to returning the pronoun to Ibrahim (peace be upon him), because his praise has already been completed. Later I saw that Hamzah al-Karmani (d. 505 AH) did the same, and he said: "until Muhammad ﷺ and the Arabs were from his loins." ﴿And upon Ishaq﴾; that is, his brother. Hamzah al-Karmani said: "until Israil (Isra'il) (the Prophet Yaqub) and the tribes (al-asbat) were from his loins." Others said: "A thousand prophets came forth from his loins, the first of whom was Ya'qub and the last of whom was Isa (peace be upon him)."

﴿And among their descendants﴾; that is, the two brothers. There is no doubt that this is closer and more fitting than that the pronoun refers to the father and the son, because mentioning the two brothers together in reporting their descendants is more appropriate than mentioning the son together with his father in that regard; thus the son would then be included among those described as the descendants of the father. ﴿is a good-doer and one who wrongs himself openly﴾; in that he placed himself, through the sins that resulted from his desires, in a position other than the one He loves. This is one of the things that undermines the assumption of natural dispositions, since the righteous is found among the wicked, and the wicked is found among the righteous.

Since a human being, however much he strives in doing good, must inevitably need forgiveness because of his shortcomings (for the rank of divinity is not reached by human limitations in fulfilling its due), He made clear that the wrongdoing intended here is only transgression of limits in pursuit of the utmost desire. So He said: ﴿openly﴾. As for anything other than that, it is forgiven, as established in verses like: ﴿It has what it earned and it bears what it has earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and the hadith: "...Whoever intends an evil deed and does not do it, a good deed is recorded for him," and: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove your minor sins from you﴾ [al-Nisa': 31].

The story of Ibrahim's sacrifice of his son (peace be upon them both) from the Torah, and the explanation that they altered it. Their translator said: (Ibrahim planted a tamarisk at Beersheba and called there on the name of the LORD, the Everlasting God. And Abraham sojourned in the land of the Philistines many days. And after these things God did tempt Abraham, and said unto him, Abraham: and he said, Behold, here I am. And he said, Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of. So Abraham rose up early in the morning, and saddled his ass, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son, and clave the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and went unto the place of which God had told him. Then on the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw the place afar off. And Abraham said unto his young men, Abide ye here with the ass; and I and the lad will go yonder and worship, and come again to you. And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering, and laid it upon Isaac his son; and he took the fire in his hand, and a knife; and they went both of them together.
