And Isaac spake unto Abraham his father, and said, My father: and he said, Here am I, my son. And he said, Behold the fire and the wood: but where is the lamb for a burnt offering? And Abraham said, My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering: so they went both of them together. And they came to the place which God had told him of; and Abraham built an altar there, and laid the wood in order, and bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar upon the wood. And Abraham stretched forth his hand, and took the knife to slay his son. And the angel of the LORD called unto him out of heaven, and said, Abraham, Abraham: and he said, Here am I. And he said, Lay not thy hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him: for now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me. And Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and behold behind him a ram caught in a thicket by his horns: and Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering in the stead of his son. And Abraham called the name of that place Jehovahjireh: as it is said to this day, In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen. And the angel of the LORD called unto Abraham out of heaven the second time, And said, By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD, for because thou hast done this thing, and hast not withheld thy son, thine only son: That in blessing I will bless thee, and in multiplying I will multiply thy seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore; and thy seed shall possess the gate of his enemies; And in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed; because thou hast obeyed my voice. So Abraham returned unto his young men, and they rose up and went together to Beersheba; and Abraham dwelt at Beersheba.) End of what they have, in its own wording. Look at it, and compare it with what preceded in "al-Baqarah" concerning the story of Isma'il and Ishaq (peace be upon them both), and you will find that they have undoubtedly altered it, because the speech contradicts itself. In this story he said: "Take your only son," and repeated the description "only" in more than one place, and this description is truly applicable only to Isma'il (peace be upon him), who was below the age of puberty. As for Ishaq (peace be upon him), he was never an only child for a moment of time, since he was born when Isma'il (peace be upon him) was thirteen years old and more, according to what they have in the Torah. His saying at the end of the story: "and in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed," fits perfectly only with Isma'il (peace be upon him). As for Ishaq (peace be upon him), only the holy lands were blessed through his seed, and only a few from other peoples followed them; rather, they themselves kept following others in worshipping idols at every turn, as their own Torah testifies, and the books of their prophets, Joshua son of Nun and those after him (peace be upon them). As for the descendants of Isma'il (peace be upon him), countless numbers of people from all nations followed them in the true religion; and after Muhammad ﷺ they did not follow any nation in worshipping other than God. Moreover, it was mentioned earlier in surah "al-Baqarah" that Sarah gave her maid Hajar (may Allah be pleased with her) to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) after he had lived in Canaan for ten years; that Isma'il (peace be upon him) was born to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) when he was eighty-six years old; that Allah (exalted be He) commanded him to be circumcised when he was ninety-nine years old; and that at that time he was given the good news of Ishaq (peace be upon him); so he circumcised Isma'il (peace be upon him) when he was thirteen years old. Then Ishaq (peace be upon him) was born to him when he was a hundred years old. Then they said the following text: (Abraham made a great feast on the day that Isaac was weaned. And Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, which she had born unto Abraham, mocking. Wherefore she said unto Abraham, Cast out this bondwoman and her son: for the son of this bondwoman shall not be heir with my son, even with Isaac. And the thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight because of his son. And God said unto Abraham, Let it not be grievous in thy sight because of the lad, and because of thy bondwoman; in all that Sarah hath said unto thee, hearken unto her voice; for in Isaac shall thy seed be called. And also of the son of the bondwoman will I make a nation, because he is thy seed. And Abraham rose up early in the morning, and took bread, and a bottle of water, and gave it unto Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, and the child, and sent her away...), until the end of what is in "al-Baqarah." Their saying "that Hagar was cast out after the weaning of Isaac, and she was carrying her son" is not correct; and it was already mentioned that his age on the day Isaac was weaned was fifteen years. It was also mentioned that Sarah ordered him to expel her while she was pregnant, that he handed her over to her, and that she drove her out, and that the angel met her and gave her the good news of Isma'il. In my copy, which is very old, nothing indicates her return. As for the version they have, it says: (The angel said to her: Return to your mistress and submit yourself under her hand); and it does not mention that she returned. The report has been established for us through the words of our Prophet ﷺ that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) placed Hajar and her son Isma'il (peace be upon him) near the Sacred House while he was still nursing; and they remained there until Hajar (may Allah be pleased with her) died; Isma'il (peace be upon him) married, and he built the House with his father (peace be upon them both). And his saying: "for in Isaac shall your seed be called" (peace be upon him) does not correspond to reality; for even if the fame of the Arabs through Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is not greater than the fame of the Children of Isaac through it, it is at least equal to it; and Allah's report does not differ. All of this shows that they altered the story and distorted it, so there is no basis for them in it. Its indication that the sacrificed one is Isma'il (peace be upon him) is stronger than any indication to the contrary, because of its description as "the only one." And Allah knows best how the story was before the alteration. Among what supports my understanding of their alteration is what al-Baghawi said: al-Qurazi (i.e., Muhammad ibn Ka'b) said: 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz asked a man who had been one of the scholars of the Jews and had embraced Islam, and whose Islam was good: Which of Ibrahim's two sons was he commanded to sacrifice? He said: Isma'il, O Commander of the Faithful; the Jews know this well, but they envy you, O Arabs, that your father, whom God commanded to sacrifice, should be what he was, and they claim that he is their father. Another proof that it was Isma'il (peace be upon him) is that when Allah (exalted be He) gave the good news of Ishaq, He gave the good news that Ya'qub would be born to him; so it is not fitting that the trial should be with him after knowing that he would not die until Ya'qub was born to him. Another proof is that the two horns of the ram were hung in the Ka'bah in the hands of the descendants of Isma'il (peace be upon him), until the House burned and the two horns burned with it in the time of Ibn al-Zubayr and al-Hajjaj. Al-Sha'bi said: "I saw the two horns of the ram hanging in the Ka'bah." And Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, at the beginning of Islam the head of the ram was still hanging by its horns in the gutter of the Ka'bah." And al-Asma'i said: "I asked Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' about the sacrificed one: was it Ishaq or Isma'il?" He said: "O Usaymi'; where has your reason gone? When was Ishaq in Makkah? It was Isma'il who was in Makkah, and he is the one who built the House with his father." End of what al-Baghawi said.

In the Book of Hajj, from the Sunan of Abu Dawud (a collection of hadith): "The Prophet ﷺ said to Uthman, who was al-Hajabi (the custodian of the Ka'bah's key), may Allah be pleased with him: 'I forgot to instruct you to cover the two horns, for it is not fitting for there to be anything in the house that distracts the one who prays.'" 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated it in his Jami' (a hadith compilation), and its wording is: "Uthman ibn Shaybah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Prophet ﷺ said to him: 'I saw the two horns of the ram, and I forgot to instruct you to cover them, for it is not fitting for there to be anything in the house that distracts one who prays.'" Thus he said: "Uthman ibn Shaybah." Perhaps it is Ibn Talhah, in which case he is the earlier one, and naming his father as Shaybah is an error; or it is Shaybah ibn Uthman, who is the cousin of the one in Abu Dawud, and so it was reversed. Allah knows best.

'Abd al-Razzaq also narrated, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "'Abd Allah ibn Shaybah ibn Uthman informed us. I asked him: 'Were there two ram's horns in the house?' He said: 'Yes, there were both in it.' I said: 'Did you see them?' He said: 'I suppose so, but 'Abd Allah ibn Babayh informed me that he had seen them.' He said: 'Others too had seen them in it.' He said: 'And they say they are the horns of the ram that Ibrahim (ʿalayhi al-salam) sacrificed.'" Ibn Jurayj said: "Safiyyah bint Shaybah said: 'The two horns of the ram were in it.'" Ibn Jurayj said: "I was told that Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: 'They were both in it.'" He said: "I was told on the authority of an old woman who said: 'I saw them in it.'"

Among what supports the view that the son was Isma'il (ʿalayhi al-salam) is Allah's (Exalted is He) description of him as "true to his promise." There is no truer promise than his fulfilment of his promise to be patient in the face of the sacrifice. Among the Children of Israel, the one who said that the son was Isma'il (ʿalayhi al-salam) was 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with him, as reported by Ibn al-Jawzi (a hadith scholar). He enumerated those who held each of the two views among the Companions and others, saying: (p. 278) "Those who held that he was Ishaq were: 'Umar, 'Ali, al-'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Musa, Abu Hurayrah, and Anas, may Allah be pleased with them all. And those who held that he was Isma'il were: Ibn 'Umar. The narration from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, differed: 'Ikrimah narrated from him that it was Ishaq, while 'Ata', Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-Jawza, and Yusuf ibn Mihran narrated from him that it was Isma'il." From this it is known that the view that he was Isma'il is preponderant, because Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, came after the senior Companions mentioned, and had they not considered it preponderant, they would not have differed from their fathers. The report of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas agreeing with his father does not undermine this; rather it supports it, because most, as you see, narrated from him the second view. Had it not been authentic to him, he would not have retracted the first, which agrees with his father's opinion, and it is for his firmness in it that he became known for it. Allah knows best.

When he had mentioned these masters, who possess the rank of detachment and purity that has already been explained, and concluded them with two brothers who never came together at all, and since one of the greatest purposes of mentioning them was to show favor to whoever has attained qualities like theirs, through nearness and victory, as consolation and encouragement for the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers who followed him, among those who, because of the severity of the trial and oppression, came close to despairing of victory, he followed them with their likes in detachment, and began with two brothers who were separated at the birth of the second, in a state in which it is ordinarily impossible for them to be together, then they were united inwardly while physically apart, then they were separated in a state in which their being together is ordinarily far-fetched, then they were united in a union from which they were never separated except by death. He began with them at the first of the two who was detached, from the time of his birth until the time of his migration (hijrah), then from the time of his return until he detached his family, who were some of the descendants of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and rescued them from the ties of the disbelievers. Then he and his brother were detached along with them from cities, towns, and most of the ties of mankind, constantly dwelling in the deserts and wastelands, where the word (of truth) is most often manifest, while God was sending to them the sources of wisdom, until they both died, upon them be the blessings, peace, greetings, and honor. Then He said, emphasizing and alerting whoever considers the victory of the believers to be impossible, coordinating with what is implied: "Then We certainly produced from them nations beyond description and beyond counting, and We bestowed favor upon many of them with kindness, from the descendants of Isma'il (peace be upon him), until 'Amr ibn Luhayy changed their religion; and from the descendants of Ishaq: Ya'qub, and the tribes (al-asbat) (peace be upon them), and whomever God willed of their offspring": ﴿And We certainly bestowed favor﴾; that is: We bestowed a favor that is definite, by what We possess of greatness, upon the first to make the tongue of truth (lisan al-sidq) prevail for Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and his progeny, a complete manifestation. He began with the two of them, with the most noble of them (as mentioned earlier) in detachment, and the more deserving of them of precedence. So He said: ﴿upon Musa﴾, one of the eminent of the detached ones, and the one who has a firm foot in that; ﴿and Harun﴾, what an eminent one! He who detached himself along with his brother, agreed with him in the most complete agreement, and supported him with the greatest support, by what the two of them brought of prophethood, the Book, and other kinds of address.

As the main purpose here is, as already passed, the station of detachment (tajarrud), and the announcement of the victory of the oppressed believers, He said: ﴿And We delivered them and their people﴾; that is, the Children of Israel. For long ages they had been in a humiliation that the humiliation of the believers among the companions of Muhammad ﷺ at the beginning of their affair does not approach; ﴿from the great distress﴾; that is, enslavement and what follows it of great miseries. This was by the destruction of the Copts, who persisted in misguidance and who were many times over the Children of Israel, until We destroyed them, so that not a single person of them escaped. Then the detachment (tajarrud) of the Children of Israel was sound at that time, and the humiliation of tyranny and rebellion was removed from them.

When He had shown the blessing of deliverance from the bondage, He followed it with the blessing of delighting in victory. So He said: ﴿And We helped them﴾; that is, Musa (Moses) and Harun (Aaron), upon them both be peace, and their people, over everyone who contended with them in that age, from Fir'awn (Pharaoh) and others; ﴿so they were the victorious﴾; that is, exclusively; ﴿the victors﴾; that is, over everyone who inflicted on them the terrible torment, namely Fir'awn and his household, and over all who opposed them or whom they opposed. So beware, O assembly of Quraysh and of the Arabs, of the like of that. The very thing against which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) warned them came to pass in the greatest measure possible; however, since our Prophet (ﷺ) was a Prophet of mercy, Allah softened their hearts until He returned them to that which they had been envied for, namely following him; and thus they became the kings of this world and the Hereafter.

Since the benefit of victory is being enabled to establish the religion, He said: ﴿And We gave them both﴾, that is, by Our might, after destroying their enemy, ﴿the Book that makes clear﴾, that is, the comprehensive, clear one, which, because of the intensity of its clarification, seeks to be clear itself. And so it is, for none of the books is like the Torah in the ease of its apprehension. Hārūn (ʿalayhi al-salām) was included with him in the pronoun, because he was like him in receiving the Book, in acting upon all that is in it, and in steadfastness upon what it calls to, although its revelation was specific to Mūsā (ʿalayhi al-salām).

﴿And We guided them to the path﴾; that is, the road clearly leading to the intended goal; ﴿the straight﴾; that is, the path which, because of its great uprightness, is as though it seeks to be upright. It is in the utmost preservation of uprightness, so it does not deviate at all. For this reason it is the laws of the upright religion.

Since good mention among those of lofty resolve and perfect determination is nobility, He said: ﴿And We left for them﴾; that is, the good praise you recognize, (p-282) ﴿among the later generations﴾; that is, everyone who comes after them until the Day of Judgment.

Since it became evident through this that the two of them possess a great station of nobility and eminence, its outcome was: ﴿Peace﴾; that is, a great peace; ﴿upon Musa﴾, the bearer of the Sharia; the one deeply rooted in embodying the purpose of the surah; ﴿and Harun﴾, his minister and his brother.

Since the victory of the Prophet ﷺ with those who were with him from among the weak, over Quraysh and all the rest of the Arabs, was—in Quraysh's view—at the utmost remoteness, and the implied sense was: "We did that for them both because of their goodness," he gave as the reason something that cuts the hearts of Quraysh, in the form of emphasis, so He said: ﴿Indeed, thus⦆ — that is, the like of this reward — ﴿We recompense⦆ — that is, always, in every age — ﴿the doers of good⦆ — that is, those firmly rooted in this attribute.

Then He gave the reason for their excellence, explained it, and emphasized it, as an encouragement toward its content and as a refutation of those who say: "The believers are not helped." He said: ﴿Indeed they are of Our servants﴾; that is, those who purified worship and submission for Us; ﴿the believers﴾; that is, those who are steadfast in the attribute of faith.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 123:

Since Ilyas was the greatest of those who stood apart from among their followers, the renewers of what had been taught of the rulings of the Torah, and since abandoning its rulings, despite the clarity with which it was described and the uprightness to which it called, had reached such an extreme of error that its like is barely believed (p-283), he pointed to the deviation from it, making clear that hearts are in the hand of Allah, glorified is He, and so He said, emphasizing: ﴿And indeed Ilyas﴾; that is, he who was one of the Children of Israel, according to all the exegetes except Ibn Mas'ud and Ikrimah, and he was of the tribe of Levi and among the descendants of Harun, peace be upon him. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: he was the paternal uncle of al-Yasa', peace be upon them. ﴿And We sent him to those among them in the land of Ba'labakk and its environs﴾; then, when they did not return to him, We removed from him the human desires and created him with angelic attributes. It is not far-fetched that the reason for naming him with this name is what had preceded in Allah's knowledge: that he would despair of those whom he called to Allah, so that he would be among those who come on the Day of Resurrection with no one beside him but one or two, as the Prophet ﷺ said, as related by the two Shaykhs: al-Bukhari, in al-Riqaq and al-Tibb, and Muslim, in al-Iman, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "The nations were shown to me; I saw the Prophet with a small group, and the Prophet with one man, and two men, and a Prophet with no one with him" (ﷺ).

So He, glorified is He, made his name fitting to his affair with his people, through his despair of them when he fled to the mountains from their evil, and their despair of being able to kill him, for they strove in that until they wearied. The clearest proof of this meaning is the reading of Ibn Amir, according to one of the transmissions from him, of joining the hamzah in continuous speech and pronouncing it with a fatha at the beginning (p-284). Although the scholars, as al-Samin related in his i'rab (grammatical analysis), said that this is the Arabs' playing with foreign names: they sometimes cut off its hamzah and at other times joined it. That is, He, glorified is He, addressed them in what they were accustomed to in their own tongue. ﴿Indeed he was among the messengers﴾; that is, to those who altered the command of the Torah and rejected what it called to.

When he said to his people: [he was] rebuking them in a way that such rebuke is due: "Will you not be mindful of God?" That is, is there in you any mindfulness (taqwa) and fear? For what you are upon entails a long evil and a severe punishment, and your being at ease and comfortable in what you are upon entails that there is no fear among you at all. This is the utmost ignorance and delusion, regarding the One of whom you know that there is no creator for you and no provider other than Him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 125:

When this rebuke served as a cause for listening, he repeated it, making its reason clear, so he said: ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l﴾; that is, a god and a lord. He is an idol that they had in the city of Ba'labakk. It was made of gold; its height was twenty cubits, and it had four faces. The Devil would enter its belly and speak the law of error, and the custodians (sadana), who numbered four hundred, would preserve it and teach it to the people. It is possible that "Ba'l" is a proper name for the aforementioned idol, in which case the second object is implied, and it was omitted so that the calling that has no similar calling would be understood, namely calling upon it as a deity. As for one who reads the irregular reading "Ba'lā'" (on the pattern of "ḥamrā'"), it is an indication of the great incitement by the king's wife to the worship of Ba'l, and to the killing of Ilyas (peace be upon him), and her husband's obedience to her in that, as al-Baghawi related. Therefore it deserved the feminine form for that reason; (p-285) it was made feminine because of her frequent involvement with it, and the species-nature is the cause of the idol.

Since their calling upon it was for worship, he clarified it with his words: ﴿and you forsake﴾. The root "w-dh-r" revolves around what is disliked, so the meaning is: and you abandon it with the abandonment of one who neglects it, one of whose traits is to be indifferent to it. Had it been said "wa-tad'ūna" (and you call), out of eagerness for paronomasia, this would not have conveyed this meaning, and the intended sense would have been reversed. Since the one who calls does not call except to remove harm or to bestow benefit, it was not permissible to call upon anyone except one who is able to annihilate whatever he wills and to bring into being whatever he desires. He said, alerting them to their error in acting and in abandoning: ﴿the best of creators﴾; that is, He is the one who needs no means in bringing into being or annihilating, so do not worship it.

Since a person knows with certainty that he did not nurture himself, neither by bringing himself into being from non-existence nor by what came after that, and since kindness is the strongest inclination in a human being, He said, making clear to those who wish to understand, reminding them of His kindness toward them and toward those who protect them and show affection to those who show affection to them, through nurturing after bringing into being from non-existence, which is the greatest nurturing, magnifying the matter and exalting it by substitution (ibdal) in the reading of the majority, with the nominative case: ﴿Allah﴾. He mentioned the Greatest Name, which comprises all attributes, as an alert that He is the absolute First, by whom alone everything came to be. ﴿your Lord﴾, that is, the One who alone is kind to you. And since they might sometimes attribute their creation to those before them, out of heedlessness or obstinacy, He said (p-286): ﴿and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones﴾, that is, those who are earliest for you; so this includes their nearer forefathers and those before them back to Adam, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 127:

Since, as has passed, among the greatest of the aims (of this surah) is consolation (al-tasliyah) and giving hope (al-tarjiyah), he (Allah) attributed as a consequence to his (Nuh's) supplication His saying: ﴿So they denied him﴾. And since the hope (of deliverance for the disbelievers) was far-fetched, he attributed as a consequence to the denial His saying, emphasizing it for the sake of (confirming) their denial: ﴿Indeed, they will surely be brought forth﴾; that is: subdued, compelled to be thrust into what We intend of punishment, the lesser and the greater; and (He) reminded them of evil and cursing for all time, even though they disliked it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 128:

﴿Except the servants of Allah﴾; that is: those who knew what is due to them of the attributes of Majesty; so they acted upon what they knew; and so they did not call upon anyone other than Him; for they did not deny [Him]. Then He described them with what He had alluded to of the description of servanthood ('ubudiyyah); and of the attribution to the Greatest Name; so He said: ﴿the sincere ones﴾; that is: [sincere] in their worship of Him; so they did not associate anything with Him, whether manifest or hidden; for they are the ones who are saved from the punishment.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 129:

When he (Abraham) struggled in the cause of Allah (Exalted is He) and carried out what was incumbent upon him of good praise, Allah (Glorified is He) rewarded him, saying, linking it to ﴿Indeed, they will be brought forth (to punishment)﴾ [al-Saffat: 127]: ﴿And We left for him﴾; that is, of the good praise, and all that would please him; ﴿among later generations﴾; that is, everyone who came after him until the Day of Recompense. And since al-Salam (peace) is a name comprising every good, because it is the manifestation of honour and the turning toward the one greeted with all that he desires, this produced His saying:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 130:

﴿Salām﴾ (Peace). Since the Arabs have several dialects in pronouncing his name, through lightening it, one of which matches the word-endings (fawāṣil) of the verses, and since there is no difference in conveying the meaning between using any of these forms, and since the form with more letters is more majestic, grander and more august, and since the context after many of his virtues calls for the utmost praise, it was best to use the form with more letters, which also matches the fawāṣil, so as to indicate his firm establishment in virtues, and to confirm that it is a non-Arabic name, not an Arabic one derived from despair (yaʼs). Although the reading of Ibn ʻĀmir, with the connecting of his hamzah, may give that impression, when he says: ﴿Upon the family of Yāsīn﴾. And whoever reads "Āli Yāsīn," it is possible that what is meant by his reading is what is meant by the other reading, because the linguists said: the āl is the person himself. And "Yāsīn" is either a dialect form of "Ilyās," or the second dialect, which is "Ilyāsīn," has been shortened, so the kasrah-bearing hamzah was dropped along with the lām. It is also possible that what is meant by "his family" is his followers, and that this would be more majestic regarding him, given what preceded it, which the context calls for. It is also possible that by this reading is intended all the prophets mentioned in this surah, of whom he is one; that is, upon the prophets mentioned after the surah of Yāsīn, indicating what their meanings called for: monotheism, prophethood, resurrection, the humbling of the disobedient, and the honouring of the obedient who has stripped himself, in love of his Lord, of all obstacles, and who cut off the strongest ties to fly toward Him. He specified this story for this, because it is the conclusion of the stories whose peace is conferred upon their people.

(p-288) When God, glorified is He, had shown the nobility of Ilyas (peace be upon him), or of the prophets of whom he is one, He gave the reason for it, emphasizing it, as a reminder that the Prophet (ﷺ) and his followers must be raised above every opponent who opposes them, even though Quraysh denied this. So He said: ﴿Indeed, thus⦆; that is, like this great reward, ﴿We reward the doers of good﴾; that is, those who are among their elite.

Then he gave the reason for the ruling by his goodness, confirming what had preceded in similar cases, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is among Our servants﴾; that is, those worthy of being attributed to Us, ﴿the believers﴾. From the emphasis is also derived an alert to the firmness of his foot in faith, and that he is in such a state that the desire to report it in this manner grows strong and the eagerness intensifies.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 134:

Since the main purpose (of this surah) is to give good news to the believers and to warn the disbelievers, and since his opponents were many while he himself was a stranger among them, He said, in the mode of majesty: ﴿When We saved him﴾; that is, despite the multitude and strength of his opponents. He did not mention them, because they were the most immersed of people in human attachments and bestial filth, which are not suitable to the purpose of this surah, which is built upon angelic attributes; ﴿and his family, all of them﴾.

Since disbelief cuts off the near kinship tie, just as belief joins the distant tie, He said: ﴿Except an old woman﴾; that is, she was his wife, for her disbelief severed her from entering into the ruling of his household. So they were stripped of her, she being ﴿among those who remained behind﴾; that is, those left behind in the dust of punishment and the evil of the final overturning.

When He had mentioned his deliverance and began with it out of concern for hope (al-tarjiya, encouraging expectation), He said, warning and expressing it with the particle of distance (for the greatness of the rank of what it entered upon), with the sense of sequence (ma'a al-tartib):

﴿Then We destroyed the others.﴾

That is: We annihilated them, by the majesty that is Ours. "The others" (al-akharin): that is, We cleared the earth of their filth, purified the blessed lands of them and of the foulness of their deeds, so that We left not one of them, and in destroying them We had no need to seek permission from anyone.

When al-Biqa'i's purpose in such passages is to warn those who oppose (the truth), and the merchants of Quraysh would pass by the site where the dwellings of the people of Lut were, namely the well-known lake, and would not take heed from them, they were counted as deniers of passing by them. So the speech was presented to them in the form of emphasis, and it was said: ﴿And indeed you﴾; that is, We did this to them, while you, O assembly of Quraysh, ﴿pass by them﴾; that is, by the places of their dwellings, on your trading journeys to Syria, ﴿in the morning﴾; that is, entering upon the morning, the time at which We overturned their cities upon them; and it is specified for the sake of reminding them of their condition at that time.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 138:

Since the night has a different appearance in terror than the day does, He said: ﴿And by night﴾; and since their situation was sufficient for the intelligent person to take warning, He rebuked them for their persistence in what had been the cause of their destruction, namely denying the adviser; so He said: ﴿Will you not then use your intellect?﴾; that is: would that you had intellects so that you might take heed from their condition, and fear the like of their end, and thus believe your Messenger. For you are more deserving than they of being seized, because he is one of you, and you know of the nobility of his lineage and the generosity of his speech and conduct, which those people did not know of their messenger.

When God, may He be exalted, had completed what He willed concerning those through whom destruction befell, whether in this world or the Hereafter, He concluded with those whose people's affair ended in safety, faith, blessing and kindness, giving precedence to hope (tarjiyah) over consolation (ta'siyah) and solace (ta'ziyah). He said, emphasizing because what comes next, the mention of the runaway (al-ibaq), might perhaps create some doubt about his affair: ﴿And indeed Yunus﴾; that is, one of the prophets of the Children of Israel, and he is Yunus ibn Matta, peace be upon him. Al-Baghawi related, in the story of Ilyas, peace be upon him, that when God, may He be exalted, sent him to a branch of the Children of Israel who were in the city of Ba'labakk, they denied him, and their king wanted to kill him. (p-291) So he hid in those mountains. He longed for people, so he came down and stayed with a woman of the Children of Israel, who was the mother of Yunus ibn Matta, peace be upon him. At that time Yunus was a suckling infant. Then he returned to the mountains, and Yunus died, peace be upon him. His mother came to those mountains and kept searching until she found Ilyas, peace be upon him. She asked him to pray for her son so that God would revive him. He said to her: "I was not commanded with this; I am only a servant who is commanded." She grieved, and her grief and supplication to him increased. So he was moved with pity for her and showed her mercy, and he went with her. He reached her house fourteen days after the death, and the boy was laid out covered in a corner of the house. So he prayed to God, and God revived him for her. Ilyas, peace be upon him, returned to his mountain. ﴿Indeed he was among the messengers﴾.

Since one of the greatest aims here is to console [the Prophet] for their arrogance toward the word of tawhid (divine oneness) and their saying, "He is a mad poet," [Allah] mentioned the matter of Yunus, peace be upon him, which shows the difficulty of the matter of prophethood, the severity of its weight, the heaviness of its burden, and the great care of Him, glory be to Him, for the messengers, peace be upon them, and that He chose them only with knowledge. So He does not abandon them, even if people strive to repel the message, so that they may grow firmer in bearing its burdens and stronger in carrying out its affair. He said: ﴿When he fled﴾; i.e., he ran away, when he was sent by his master, whom Allah had honored with the message, out of weakness in bearing it. Ibaq (fleeing) is running away from one's master to a place where one thinks he will remain hidden from him. ﴿To the ship﴾; i.e., the vessel in which one travels on the back of the sea. [p. 292]

Since his act resembled the act of one who is hostile, and his intention was to go far away and to hasten his departure, He said: ﴿The laden﴾; i.e., filled to capacity, so that there is no room in it for anything else. Its people therefore had no need to stay even for a moment to wait for anything. When he placed his foot in it, they set sail, and the affair became turbulent for them and the upheaval grew great, until their vessel was on the verge of sinking. They recognized, by the condition they were in, that this was because of a slave who had fled from his master, for among the people of the sea it is believed that a ship's course does not stay steady if there is a runaway aboard. This was related by al-Karmani and others, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. This caused them to cast lots (al-musahamah); i.e., to draw lots, as is their custom in such a matter. So they cast lots.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 141:

﴿Then he cast lots﴾; that is, Yunus (peace be upon him) drew lots with them. Al-Baghawi said: al-musahama (casting lots) is the casting of arrows by way of drawing lots. And when the outcome of the drawing of lots came to mean that he would be thrown from the ship, from a high place to a low one, he expressed this by using a term that indicates slipping, which occurs from a height to a lower place. So he said, as a consequence of the casting of lots: ﴿and he was among the losers﴾; that is, those who were made to slip into misfortune (al-dahd), which is slipping. Thus he came down from the place of success when the lot fell upon him, and they threw him into the sea.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 142:

﴿So the fish swallowed him﴾; i.e., it swallowed him as a morsel is swallowed; ﴿the fish﴾; i.e., the well-known one; in that it has no fish larger than it, so it is as if there were no other fish; (p-293) ﴿while he was blameworthy﴾; i.e., while the state of Yunus (peace be upon him) was that he had entered into blame.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 143:

When what happened happened, he stripped himself of himself and of others, with a stripping that no one else had matched in its totality. Therefore he increased in this stripping by annihilating (fana') in the station of oneness (wahdaniyyah), and he persisted in transcendence (tanzih), until Allah (Exalted is He) delivered him. The indication of this is in the saying of Allah (Exalted is He): ﴿Had he not been one of those who glorify Allah﴾; that is, by creation and by character; ﴿of those who glorify (musabbihin)﴾; that is, those who are deeply immersed (ariqin) in this station. This is what the word "tasbih" (glorification) can rightly be applied to in the language: transcendence of Allah with the heart, the tongue, and the limbs, through prayer and other acts, because his creation conforms to what his character was prepared for. So he was constant in that in times of ease, comfort, lowliness, and abundance; how much more so, then, in times of hardship. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) interpreted it as prayer.

﴿Then he would have remained in its belly﴾; that is, alive. Or, he would have become its nourishment, so that his parts would have mixed with its parts. ﴿Until the Day they are resurrected﴾; that is, he and the fish and other creatures. He used the plural to indicate the generality of the resurrection. Had he used the singular, it would not have conveyed the resurrection of the dumb animals. Had he used the dual, it would have been thought that this applied only to him and the fish, for a specific reason pertaining to the two of them, and so it would not convey the resurrection of anything else. It has also been said: ﴿he would have remained alive in its belly﴾. In the verse there is an allusion to the hadith: "Get to know God in ease, and He will know you in hardship," and an exhortation to remembrance (dhikr), and a magnification of His station. (p-٢٩٤)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 145:

Since the implied sense is: but because he was one who remembered God in times of ease, We remembered him in the time of distress; so We rescued him from his belly and brought him out from it unharmed. That was a matter striking to the intellect, and He displayed it in the manifestation of greatness, saying: ﴿So We cast him﴾; that is, We threw him out of the belly of the fish, with a casting that was not the same for anyone else, and that was easy for Us; ﴿onto the open shore﴾; that is, the barren, wide place, devoid of any cover of vegetation or otherwise; and that was on the shore of Mosul. Abu Hayyan said: He cast him in Nisibis, on the side of Mosul; ﴿while he was sick﴾; that is, very weak, from what had befallen him in the belly of the fish, such that he was like a child at the hour of its birth; and he was then, nonetheless, praiseworthy and not blameworthy, by the grace of God that overtook him; so he was chosen, and among the righteous.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 146:

﴿And We caused to grow﴾; that is: by Our greatness; in that place, which has no inherent capacity for growth whatsoever; let alone for what cannot grow except with abundant water.

And since his affliction was extreme, reaching a degree that is beyond description, He drew attention to it with the particle of elevation; so He said: ﴿over him﴾; that is: and We raised it above him at the time of causing it to grow, so that it would shade him as a house shelters a person. And since the gourd (al-dubba') is of the category of the star-plant (al-najm), and He, glorified is He, had magnified it for his sake, He described it by what has a stem, so He said: ﴿a tree﴾; and since this expression might be understood as meaning something with a stem, He specified the departure from custom by His saying: (p-295) ﴿of gourd (yaqtin)﴾; that is: of the trees that cling to the earth, that dwell in it, and that are suitable for one to take refuge under and dwell beside, until his condition is set right; for He, may He be exalted, magnified it and removed it from the custom of its kind, until it became over him like a trellis. And "al-yaqtin" is: everything that spreads and extends over the surface of the earth, does not persist through winter, and does not stand on a stem, such as the watermelon and the cucumber. What is meant here, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said, is the gourd plant, because of the size of its leaves, the coolness of its shade, the smoothness of its surface, and that flies do not approach it. Abu Hayyan said: its leaf-water, when sprinkled on a place, means that no fly approaches that place at all. Others said: there is a compatibility in it with the human body, such that if a bone is lost from his head and a piece of gourd skin is placed in its stead, flesh grows upon it and fills its place. And it is from "qatana bil-makan," when one resides in a place with the residence of one who is passing through, not one who is settled.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 147:

Since the consideration of the tarjiyah (the hope of a good outcome) is greater, He concluded with it, as an indication that He will not cause the Prophet (ﷺ) to die until He gratifies his eye with his community, in great numbers, in obedience and blessing. So He said: ﴿And We sent him﴾, i.e., by Our majesty, before which nothing can stand. And since the purpose does not depend on specifying the people to whom he was sent, or whether they are those from whom he had fled or not, He said: ﴿to a hundred thousand﴾. The majority hold that they are the ones to whom he was first sent, as Abu Hayyan said. And since a large number cannot be fixed by the observer at its exact count, but he will say, even if he is the most firm of people in his judgment, "they are such-and-such, a little more or less," and at times he will affirm that they are not fewer than such-and-such, while an increase is possible; and at times his opinion inclines toward an increase, and this is what is intended here, He said: ﴿or they increase﴾, because hope in the multiplication of followers is more comforting to the eye and more delightful to the heart, and to make clear that the increase has occurred. These people to whom he was sent are the people of Nineveh, and they were not of his own people, for the borders of the land of the Children of Israel extend to the Euphrates, while Nineveh lies to the east of the Euphrates, very far from it.

(p. 297) ﴿So they believed﴾, meaning that they stripped themselves of worldly appetites and joined the angelic attributes. And since their belief was the cause of the lifting of the punishment that their disbelief had made due for them, He said: ﴿So We gave them enjoyment﴾, meaning that while We remain as We are in Our greatness, that did not diminish Our greatness in any way, nor did it add to it; ﴿for a time﴾, meaning until the end of the terms We had appointed for them from eternity.

Mention of the story of Yunus (peace be upon him) from the Book of the Prophets. Its translator said: With the help and strength of God, we begin by transcribing the prophecy of Yunan ibn Matta (Jonah son of Amittai), the Prophet. The word of the Lord came to Yunan ibn Matta, saying to him: "Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry out against it, for their wickedness has come up before Me." But Yunan rose to flee to Tarsis from the presence of the Lord, and he went down to Joppa, and found a ship that was going to Tarsis. So he paid the sailor his fare and went down into it to go with them to Tarsis, fleeing from the presence of the Lord. But the Lord cast a great wind upon the sea, so there was a great storm on the sea, and the ship was about to break apart. The sailors were afraid, and every man cried out to his god, and they threw the cargo of the ship into the sea to lighten it for themselves. But Yunan had gone down into the lowest part of the ship and lay down and fell asleep. So the captain of the sailors came to him and said to him: "Why are you sleeping? Arise, call upon your God; perhaps God will save us, so that we do not perish." And the men said to one another: "Come, let us cast lots, and we shall know on whose account this evil has come upon us." So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Yunan. They said to him: "Tell us, on whose account is this evil upon us? What is your occupation? Where do you come from? What is your people? And what is your land?" (p. 298) He said to them: "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land." Those men were terribly afraid, and they said to him: "What have you done?" For those men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of his God, because he had told them. Then they said: "What shall we do with you, so that the sea may be calm for us?" For the sea was growing more violent against us. He said to them: "Take me up and throw me into the sea, and the sea will be calm for you, for I know that this great storm has come upon you because of me." But those men struggled to row back to the shore, yet they found no way, for the sea was growing more violent against them. Then they called upon the Lord and said: "O Lord, do not let us be held guilty for the blood of this innocent man, and do not let us perish on account of this man's life, for You, O Lord, do whatever You will." So they took Yunan and threw him into the sea, and the sea ceased its raging. Those men feared the Lord greatly, and they offered sacrifices to the Lord and made vows to Him. The Lord prepared a great fish, which swallowed Yunan, and Yunan was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights. And he said: "I cried to the Lord in my distress, and He answered me; from the belly of Sheol I cried out, and He heard my voice. He cast me into the depths, into the heart of the sea, and the floods surrounded me; all Your waves and billows passed over me. (p. 299) I said: 'I have been cast out from before Your eyes; yet I shall again look upon Your holy temple.' The waters surrounded me even to my soul; the deep closed around me; weeds were wrapped about my head. I went down to the bottoms of the mountains; the earth with its bars closed behind me forever. When my soul fainted within me, I remembered the Lord, and my prayer came to You, into Your holy temple. Those who regard vain idols forsake their own mercy. But I will sacrifice to You with the voice of thanksgiving; what I have vowed I will pay. Salvation is from the Lord." So the Lord commanded the fish, and it vomited Yunan onto the dry land. The word of the Lord came to Yunan a second time, saying to him: "Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and proclaim to it the message that I tell you." So Yunan arose and went to Nineveh, according to the word of the Lord. Nineveh was an exceedingly great city before God, a three days' journey across. Yunan began to enter the city a day's journey, and he cried out, saying: "Forty days more, and Nineveh shall be overthrown." The people of Nineveh believed in God; they proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from their greatest to their least. The word reached the king of Nineveh, and he rose from his throne, (p. 300) and took off his robe, clothed himself in sackcloth, and sat in ashes. He proclaimed in Nineveh, saying: "By decree of the king and his nobles: let neither men nor herds, flocks nor beasts taste anything; let them not graze nor drink water. But let men and beasts be covered with sackcloth, and let them call upon God mightily; let every man turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands. Who knows whether God will turn and relent, and turn away from His fierce anger, so that we do not perish?" God saw their deeds, that they had turned from their evil ways, so He relented from the punishment He had threatened, and did not bring it upon them. But Yunan was greatly grieved and very displeased, and he prayed before the Lord and said: "O Lord, was this not my word while I was still in my own country? That is why I hastened to flee to Tarsis. I knew truly that You are the gracious and merciful God, slow to anger, abundant in kindness, who relents from evil. Now, O Lord, take my soul from me, for death is better for me than life." The Lord said to him: "Are you very angry, Yunan?" Yunan went out from the city and made for himself a booth there, and he sat under it in the shade, to see what would become of the city. God appointed a gourd plant, and it grew up over Yunan's head to be a shade for his head, to deliver him from his discomfort. And Yunan rejoiced greatly over the gourd. (p. 301) But the next morning God sent a worm at dawn, which struck the gourd so that it withered. When the sun rose, God sent a scorching east wind, and the sun beat upon Yunan's head so that he grew faint, and he asked for death for himself, saying: "It is better for me to die than to live." God said to Yunan: "Are you very angry about the gourd?" He said: "I am very angry, even to death." The Lord said: "You had pity on the gourd, for which you did not labor and which you did not grow; it came up in a night and perished in a night. Should I not have pity on Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know their right hand from their left, and much livestock?" End of quotation.

Perhaps the gourd mentioned here had grown on him when he came out of the belly of the fish; when what is mentioned here happened to him, he returned to it, and it had grown large, so he built an arbor beneath it and sat beneath it, and what happened, happened. Therefore what is mentioned here does not contradict what the people of reports have mentioned in this story. And God is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 149:

Since what was previously asserted were two matters: first, that these warned ones (al-mundharun) hasten to follow the traces of their fathers in misguidance; and second, that most of the earlier people went astray. These six narratives were brought as a witnessed proof (dalil shuhudi) for the second matter, of which the only people from among them who were guided as a whole community were the people of Yunus, upon him be peace. This became the reason for the command to establish the proof of the misguidance of these people, who follow their fathers, with a command that is in the clarification of error no clearer than it. So He said, mocking them and specifying the command to him (ﷺ), as an indication of the greatness of this outcome, and that no one comprehends it in its true comprehension except him (ﷺ): ﴿So ask them (fastaftihim)﴾; that is: ask of these who turn away from your call toward their falsehoods, that they answer you, out of nobility and generosity: by what proof and by what argument did they judge, by following their fathers, concerning the angels, whom it was stated in "Fatir" that they are the messengers of God, and in "Ya-Sin" that they are in the utmost severity, such that the punishment of a large nation is sufficed by one of them, and such that a single cry from one of them causes all the living to die, and another cry brings all the dead back to life? In addition to what this surah has conveyed to them of lining up, of admonition, and of recitation, when it began with an oath by them, because its aim has a great regard for their states in their detachment and sanctification. It entails from this questioning their exoneration, and the exoneration of the One who created them, and that is the aim of the surah. He turned the speech from the manifestation of greatness to what is a proof of it, for the messenger indicates the rank of the one who sent him. So He said: ﴿To your Lord (alirabbika)﴾; that is: specifically; He is the Supreme King, who raised you and bestowed kindness upon you by guiding you, and by guiding through you, and other than that of your affairs, until you were the most perfect of creation and the highest of them in every matter by which perfection and nearness to God is attained; so He chose you for His message. Thus in the singularity of the pronoun there is an indication that He chooses only the most perfect, the most noble, and the most excellent.

Since the intent was to rebuke them, by their making the lowest share for God, and since females are weaker than males, yet the term "female" (unutha) may be applied to other than animals, and females in some kinds, such as the fragrant plants (al-asḥar), are more noble, he turned away from expressing it with "females" and expressed with what explicitly states the intent, so He said: ﴿The daughters (al-banat)﴾; that is: rather than the sons; and they, despite being subjects and subdued, disdain them to the utmost disdain; ﴿and for them﴾; that is: rather than Him; ﴿the sons (al-banun)﴾. Although the Lord, whom they assigned to the lesser of the two kinds, at times creates the male from dust and raises him in the best upbringing, and at other times from something else, or brings him out from the belly of a fish, or from the depths of fire, or otherwise; by what means, then, did they claim a child for Him, when a child only comes about gradually through the stages of creation, from a drop of semen to what is above it, and none is content with that except one who is weak? How then with claiming the lesser of the two kinds of offspring? Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might.

When their claim that the angels are female included a claim to knowledge of the matter, because the claim of offspring was made with the lesser of the two categories, or a claim to knowledge that He created them female through witnessing them, or through a book from Him to them, and as for reason, it has no role in this, He said, informing that they are people who deserve to be rebuked and mocked, because they have no knowledge of either of the two ways, and they cannot claim this lest they be exposed to a disgrace that can never be remedied at all, returning to the explicit mention of the mark of greatness, indicating that it is in the nature of such things to be densely veiled: ﴿Or did We create﴾, that is, by virtue of the greatness We possess, which, if it does not require choosing the most perfect, does not require singling out the inferior, because it is incompatible with lowliness in every respect; ﴿the angels﴾, that is, those whom they judged to be female, and they are among the greatest of Our messengers and the most exalted of Our chosen ones, and they did not see any of them, and there is no way for them to know their states, as they themselves acknowledge; and since it became clear that what is meant by femaleness is baseness, and some females have the strength of males, He expressed it as femaleness, binding them, in their judgment, to two baseness: ﴿females while﴾, that is, while the state is that these people who attribute to Allah what is not befitting Him; ﴿they are witnesses﴾, that is, the witnessing of that is established for them, they are not absent from it, for We renew from among them whomever We will each day. Al-Razi said: Each of the angels is a species of its own, while the children of Adam are all one species, which is deficient at the beginning of its natural disposition and is perfected, and has degrees of ascent, until it reaches the station of witnessing, which is that there is manifested to it the adornment of the First Truth from His essence, His attributes, and the ordering of His acts, with a knowledge that does not separate from it, and does not vanish, so that in its perception it ascends above the sensible things and the imaginings, and its action ascends above being for the sake of the demand of anger or desire; and by this one draws near to Allah (Exalted); ends.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 151:

When the listener's eagerness to know the true meaning of their statement, which gave rise to this questioning, became intense, He—glory be to Him—informed them of that in His saying, emphasizing it (to indicate that it is a statement that hardly anyone would admit having made), expressing wonder at them concerning it, and calling out against them with what He had made clear of their disgrace through the questioning they had already put forward: ﴿Surely they are of their own falsehood﴾; that is, because their habit is to turn matters away from their proper aspects, ﴿they say﴾; that is, a statement they persist in, even if they are not able to express it openly in a context of debate. He turned away from the manifest form of majesty to the proper name of Majesty (Allah), which denotes the Essence that comprises all attributes, to indicate that every attribute of His and every quality of His rejects the notion of having a son. So He said:

﴿He has begotten a son﴾: that is, there came into existence for Him, the One encompassing all attributes of perfection, a child. They are in the attribute of femininity, meaning that He brought forth a child. Thus *walada* is a past-tense verb (*fi'l madi*), and *al-Jalalah* (the Divine Name, Allah) is its subject (*fa'il*). It was read anomalously (*shadhdh*) with *walada* in the nominative, as the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), and with the Name in the genitive through the construct (*idafah*). The word *walad* is of the pattern *fa'al* in the sense of *maf'ul*, like *qabad*. Therefore it is predicated of the singular and other than the singular, and of the feminine and other than the feminine.

When He, glorified is He, mentioned the Greatest Name (*al-Ism al-A'zam*), as an indication of His supreme exaltation above that, He made it explicit in His saying, indicating permanence and emphasizing it because of their claim, that they are truthful: ﴿Indeed, they are liars﴾.

It also indicated their falsehood by His disavowal of it, rebuking them in the manner of address, to increase their vexation, in His saying: ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ with the interrogative hamzah of disavowal (p-306). Whoever omits it, the hamzah is in his view implied and intended, meaning: Tell me, has this Lord—whose complete knowledge, all-encompassing power, and supreme lordship you acknowledge—chosen for Himself what you yourselves consider inferior?

Since expressing it as "daughters" (al-bint) was more hateful to them than expressing it as "female" (al-untha), and expressing it as "sons" (al-ibn) was more beloved to them than expressing it as "males" (al-dhukur), and in order to state the intended meaning explicitly—because the word "male" (al-dhakar) is shared among several meanings—He said: ﴿daughters﴾, whose attachment to you you disdain, and whose association with you you find shameful, to the point that some of you go so far in getting rid of them as to bury them alive; ﴿over sons﴾. Thus His regard for Himself was then His own, not the regard of the least of you, let alone the greatest of you. For this reason, His saying was greatly beautiful and supremely eloquent.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 154:

﴿Mā﴾; that is: O assembly of the Arabs who claim soundness of intellect, correctness of judgment and sound understanding, what ﴿lakum﴾ (is the matter with you)? What good is there for you in this speech? Then he increased the rebuke against them with his saying, marveling at them: ﴿Kayfa tahkumūn﴾ (How do you judge?); that is, regarding everything we have asked you about, with judgments of this kind, which do not proceed from anyone who has even the least grip on his intellect. He expressed it with "judgment" (ḥukm) because it is well known in matters that are decided, so it refuses deficiency; therefore expressing it with that term was greater in rebuking them, since they applied it to what is weaker than anything.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 155:

When this was extremely contrary to the intellects and far removed from natural dispositions, his saying, also in rebuke, was most fitting: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾; that is, even the slightest remembrance, by what the reading of the one who lightened (the form) indicated, through what it gathered of lightening and elision; for the matter is in the utmost clarity (p-307) to what is in your intellects and dispositions, that you do not accept for yourselves the lowest of positions. So how would your Lord, in whose hand is everything, choose it for Himself? Indeed, a child in absolute terms is only from one who has a kind (jins), so he would be in need of his kind; and one who is in need cannot be a god in any respect. The reading of the community with the doubling and idgham (assimilation) indicated that the matter requires greater remembrance, by what the doubling indicated, together with subtlety, by what the idgham indicated, for the sake of resolving the doubt of one who sees the acts of one who buries alive the infant girl and thinks that this is a desire on their part for females; but that is nothing other than a desire to repel the corruption of killing and out of mercy for the weak. It was not read with the unassimilated form (fakk), indicating that the matter is independent of the highest level of reflection.

When al-Biqa'i had established their witnessing of this (by what it implied, namely the refutation of it by reason), so that no path of proofs remained except revelation (al-sam'), he balanced with it His saying: ﴿Or do you have a authority?﴾; that is, for the claim of that; ﴿an authority﴾; that is, a revealed proof (dalil sam'i), by a heavenly report that is conclusive; and he indicated that one does not speak about the affairs of kings except with a clear matter, by His saying: ﴿clear﴾.

Since what is meant by this, necessarily, is the revealed proof (al-burhan al-sam'i), he clarified it by what follows from his saying: ﴿So bring your Book﴾; that is, the one that brought you that authority from the King, regarding His having chosen that for Himself. He indicated their falsehood allusively after having stated it explicitly, and the most piercing way of doing so was by using the particle of doubt in His saying: ﴿if you are truthful﴾. These verses proceed from great wrath and terrible denial, and the styles in which they came speak plainly of the folly of the one who claims this, of the ignorance of their souls and the feebleness of their minds, together with mockery, derision, and amazement that such a thing could occur to anyone's mind, let alone be adopted as a belief and openly held as a doctrine.

When the manifestation of their misguidance was complete, He rebuked them in another style, turning away from addressing them directly, as a warning of the descent of His punishment upon them. So He said: ﴿And they made﴾; that is, some of the Arabs, who rejected the proofs whose explanation has already passed, ﴿between Him and the jinn﴾; that is, the jinn, who are the most evil of the classes (of beings), ﴿a kinship﴾. He made them feminine, as an indication of their contemptibility in this matter for which they qualified them. They said that He, may the radiance of His Face be exalted and His majesty be magnified, exalted is His majesty, married the daughters of the chieftains of the jinn, and so He begot the angels from them. It is well known that no one marries except someone of his own kind, so they went to the furthest extreme of distance, because He has no kind like Him. Since kinship is something honoured and not disgraced, He said, making their pronoun feminine to add to their contemptibility: ﴿And the jinn have certainly known﴾; that is, absolutely, the chieftains among them and the lowly ones, ﴿that they﴾; that is, all of the jinn, ﴿will surely be brought forth﴾; that is, before Him, for resurrection, unwillingly, so that they may be dealt with justly, along with the rest of creation, on the Day of the Decisive Judgement, and the manifestation of might, greatness and majesty. So they are too lowly to be claimed to have this (kinship).

(p-309) When he mentioned the Greatest Day, on which the bonds of attributes become manifest to everyone, the essences of existing things vanish at its manifestations, and the traces of perishable things are effaced before its qualities, and when his mention of it was in a clear manner, far removed from unsuitability, it became a means of tanzih (exalting God above all imperfection), and after those misguidances, a place for taqdis (sanctification) as a result of that. So he said, explicitly naming tasbih (glorification), which comprises all its kinds, and the Majesty (al-Jalalah), indicating the greatness of the station: ﴿Glory be to God﴾; i.e., exalted is He who possesses all greatness, with a transcendence that exceeds all limits; ﴿above what they describe﴾; i.e., above what all creatures describe Him with, those whom the gathering brings together on that day; or the disbelievers who ascribed offspring to Him and made the angels among the offspring.

ﷻ "Except the servants of Allah" (ﷻ). That is, those who are fit to be attached to the Greatest Name, in terms of its being applied to the Greatest Essence (al-Dhat al-A'zam). For this reason he used the apparent noun and did not use a pronoun, because a pronoun would refer to the very same thing mentioned before, and so it might give the impression that their honouring is restricted to what was mentioned in the first instance, so that the honouring of them would be understood as restricted to glorification (tasbih).

"The sincere ones" (al-mukhlasin): from among all creatures; or from among the Arabs, namely those of them who embraced Islam after the revelation of this sura, for they describe Him only with what has been permitted to them concerning Him. And because this sura is the sura of those who strip themselves of the ties of the obstacles to journeying toward Him, he repeated the description of sincerity (al-ikhlas) in it many times.

When al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) has declared the Holy Essence, glorified be He, free of every deficiency, he indicated this by stating that they and all that they worship besides Him are unable to do anything He has not decreed. So he said—making it a consequence of the declaration of His transcendence, emphasizing it, refuting those who suppose that other than Allah possesses anything, and addressing them directly with the speech, since that is more stinging and more fitting to provoke anger—﴿So indeed you and what you worship﴾; that is, of the idols and others, of everyone you have claimed to be a god. He began the predicate with "inna" (indeed/verily, a particle of emphasis), and prefaced it with the negating element, saying:

Surah 37, verse 162 (al-Biqa'i, Nazm al-Durar):

﴿Mā﴾ (ma, "what"). He gave precedence to the addressees, expressed by the second-person pronoun (kaf al-khitab), over those they were joined with in the conjunction, namely their objects of worship. This is to alert the reader that these objects are nothing (ʿadam). Likewise, he belittled them by referring to them with ﴿mā﴾ rather than ﴿man﴾ (who). So He said, addressing them: ﴿You, you cannot lead astray concerning Him﴾; that is, concerning Allah alone; ﴿anyone﴾ — that is, you cannot make any of the people deviate by misguidance.

﴿Except for him who is﴾; i.e., within His judgment and decree, ﴿destined to burn in Hellfire﴾; i.e., tormented by its punishment, because He has judged him to wretchedness. Thus it is known that you cannot cause him to change, except one whom He Himself has changed. By His judgment he went astray, not by you. "We seek refuge in You from You; there is no escape from You except to You." The purpose of placing the prepositional phrase first is that another may be able to corrupt one whom he does not want corrupted, while being unable to repel the corrupter. So the expression with the particle of elevation (ʿalā, "over") is a mockery of them, meaning: you have no power of misguidance except this that He has made for you as a means. If you have dominance, then name it by that. The uniformity of the pronoun with the word "man" (whoever) in both places indicates that those who die in polytheism among the Arabs after the sending of the Prophet (ﷺ) are few. It was read irregularly (shādhdh, a reading not meeting the conditions of the accepted recitations) as "ṣāluw" (صالُو), to dispel the assumption that it is singular.

(p-311) Since it is well known that this consultation (istif'a) from the Prophet ﷺ took place in compliance with the command that preceded it, and by this sentence their power was nullified, as was the power of the objects of their worship, to which they ascribe some power, he said, emphasizing this and nullifying also the power of the sincere ones (al-mukhlisin), coordinated with ﴿So indeed you and what you worship﴾ [as-Saffat: 161]: ﴿And there is none of us﴾, that is: we, you, your objects of worship, and anyone other than these, ﴿except that he has a known station﴾, which God (Exalted is He) had decreed from eternity. Then He informed the angels of what He willed concerning it. So no one among creation can exceed what He has established for him in any manner of transgression, may He be glorified. Each of the angels has a known station that he does not go beyond. The saints (al-awliya') have a hidden station between them and God, which no one perceives. The prophets, upon them be prayer and peace, have a well-known station, supported by manifest miracles, because they are a model (qudwa) for creation; so their matter is one of public renown (al-shuhra), while the matter of the saints is one of concealment (al-sutra). This was said by al-Qushayri. As for those other than those mentioned, from among the people of happiness, they have a station in wretchedness that is known to God (Exalted is He) and to whomever of His servants He informs of it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 165:

When He had stripped all of them of every power except what He had granted them, and the disbelievers claimed that they worship Allah (exalted is He) and glorify Him, and that associating partners with Him does not detract from that, He made clear that the sincere ones (al-mukhlasun) were singled out, apart from them, for stations of purity and ranks of truthfulness and fidelity, because their obedience was nullified by their associating partners with Him. So He said, emphasizing and specifying: ﴿And indeed, it is We who are the ones lined up in rows﴾; that is, O assembly of the sincere ones, ﴿it is We﴾, that is, to the exclusion of you, ﴿who are the ones lined up in rows﴾; that is, we set ourselves in rows in prayer and in jihad, and our wings spread out in the air in carrying out what We have been sent with, and otherwise, because our hearts are gathered together upon obedience;

﴿And indeed, it is we who are the ones who glorify (Him)﴾; that is, we who declare Him—exalted is He—free from every deficiency that you have attributed to Him, such as daughters. It is also possible that the meaning is: this action belongs to us, namely the lining up in rows and the glorifying (tasbih), and it is not intended to have any object at all.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 167:

When he had made clear their misguidance, and the guidance of him (ﷺ) and the guidance of those who follow him, by what he indicated through the attribute of Lordship, which he attributed to himself in His saying: ﴿Is it for your Lord...﴾, he informed that they had added to the defect of misguidance in itself the defect of breaking promises and violating the covenant they had solemnly affirmed. So He said, emphasizing (this), as an indication that it is hardly credible that a rational person would make a firm pledge to himself about a matter and then break it, in answer to one who says: Did they declare Him free of (such things) as the sincere servants declared Him free?: ﴿And indeed﴾, i.e., they did this out of misguidance through doubts that have been exposed, by what We have uncovered of their veils, and they did not declare Him free as the sincere servants did; and the state is that they ﴿were﴾ before this ﴿saying﴾, i.e., a saying they never stopped renewing, along with what it contains of emphasis.
﴿Had we had with us a reminder﴾; that is, in whatever state it might have been, whether a Book or otherwise; ﴿from the former ones﴾; that is, from the earlier messengers who passed away;

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 169:

﴿Surely we would have been the servants of Allah﴾; that is, in such a way that we would become fit to be attributed to the One who encompasses all the attributes of perfection; ﴿the sincere ones﴾; that is, in worshipping Him, without any admixture of association (shirk) whatsoever.

When this Reminder (dhikr) that came to them—together with its being the greatest of reminders—came confirming the scriptures of the earlier peoples, and the Messenger who brought it was the greatest of the messengers, then it was, for that very reason, along with the added nobility, the cause of their disbelief in what they had pledged themselves to. So He said: ﴿So they disbelieved in it﴾. That is: as a consequence of what they had pledged, they disbelieved in that Reminder, despite its being more noble than what they had asked for, in terms of its inimitability and other qualities. Consequently, there followed a threat against them, from those who broke their promise and violated their covenant after emphasizing it. So He said: ﴿But they will soon know﴾. That is: with a threat that is not of the same kind as their own speech, but rather is something in which there is no failure in any way.

(p-314) Since the implied sense, as the context of threat indicates, is: "Indeed Our word has already preceded against those who opposed Our messengers with humiliating abandonment," He follows it with His saying: ﴿And indeed Our word has preceded﴾, i.e., in eternity; ﴿Our word﴾, i.e., in accordance with the majesty that belongs to Us; ﴿to Our servants﴾, i.e., those who devoted their worship sincerely to Us in every movement and stillness; ﴿the messengers﴾, those whom We added, to the honor of sincerity in servanthood, the honor of messengerhood.

Now that the lam (of emphasis) has signaled their exaltedness, he clarified this by explaining what he called "a word" (kalimah), because it is united in one meaning, by his saying: ﴿Indeed they﴾; and he increased its emphasis, in contrast to what is with the disbelievers, in accordance with what their deeds indicate of his being in the utmost distance; so he said: ﴿Surely they﴾, that is, exclusively; ﴿are the ones given victory﴾, that is, whose victory is constant in argument and in combat, even if the disbelievers gain some ascendancy over them in the latter.

And since he restricted this to the messengers, he generalized, so he said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 173:

﴿And indeed Our hosts﴾; that is, from among the messengers and those who follow them. Since the meaning of jund (hosts) in the language is the army, the helpers, and the (vanguard) city, and a category of creation distinct on its own, He said, combining them in meaning rather than in wording, as an explicit statement of the intended sense: ﴿they, they are the victorious﴾; that is, not others than them. ﴿The victorious﴾; that is, even if it is seen that they are defeated, because the final outcome is theirs, if not in this abode then in the abode of permanence. This noble Prophet was granted both of these, and He called all of this "a word" (kalimah) because it is unified in one meaning. A defeat in some of the battlegrounds on the part of some of them does not harm, nor does a weakness that may occur. And sufficient as evidence for this is the (p-315) biography of the Prophet ﷺ and the three Rightly-Guided Caliphs after him, may Allah be pleased with them.

Now that it has been firmly established, by this, that he (ﷺ) is the one granted victory, because he is among the messengers and among God's army, indeed the highest of them, the consequence of that is His saying: ﴿So turn away from them﴾; that is, impose upon yourself the turning away; ﴿from them﴾; that is, from trying to turn them back from misguidance by force; ﴿for a time﴾; that is, an undetermined time, which is the time We appointed for your victory from eternity.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 37, verse 175:

﴿And observe them﴾; that is: with your sight and your insight, at the time We have appointed for you. Before it: how their conditions and their fluctuations will be, whenever they turn about toward decline.

And since before Islam they were blind and deaf, because they do not believe a promise or a threat, and do not reflect on the outcome, He omitted the object of their verb. So He said, threatening them, confirming with the future particle (sawfa) — not distancing [the matter]: ﴿so they will see﴾; that is: there will come to them the sight that admits no error, with the eye and with the heart, after what they are in of blindness. This time is clearly [fulfilled] on the day of "Badr," and what was similar to it before the conquest (fath). For they had, in those times, a kind of strength, and so He affirmed for them a kind of sight in their seeing.

Since it was their habit to hasten toward that with which they were threatened, mocking it, whenever a threat came to them, He therefore based upon that a denunciation of them, in the form of another threat against them, and said: ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ That is, in light of the greatness known of it through its attribution to Us; (p-316) ﴿they seek to hasten﴾, that is, they request that it be hastened for them, so that it comes to them before its appointed time which We have set for it.

When this was understood, that there will be no good tidings for them on the day it descends upon them, nor any settling place when it comes down, He stated this explicitly in His words: ﴿So when﴾, that is: We threaten them and rebuke them, because when it ﴿descends into their courtyard﴾, that is: overcomes it.
